1 Getting MICS6 data This guide focuses on Round 6 of UNICEF’s Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS6), the round in which the Foundational Learning Skills (FLS) module was introduced. There are two main ways to obtain MICS6 data for the analyses covered in this guide: UNICEF MICS — download the original country datasets released by UNICEF; or IPUMS MICS — create a customised, harmonised multi-country extract using the IPUMS MICS data system. Both routes are useful. Which one you should use depends on your research question and, especially, whether you need the foundational reading data. Two practical constraints also matter: building an IPUMS MICS extract currently requires a Stata licence, and if you are analysing a single country the harmonisation that IPUMS provides adds little. 1.1 Which source should I use? The resulting .dta can then be analysed in either R or Stata Single-country analysis Recommended Adds little: the benefit of IPUMS is cross-survey harmonisation Foundational numeracy Recommended Can be used Foundational reading Recommended Do not use the IPUMS reading variables in MICS6 surveys with multiple reading passages. IPUMS retains only one passage, so children assessed on other passages are missing from the harmonised reading variables. See Adding the correct reading data to an IPUMS extract for the AFLEARN solution. AFLEARN recommendation If your analysis uses foundational reading outcomes, do not use the IPUMS reading variables for countries that administered more than one reading passage. IPUMS retains only one passage, which can exclude a large share of children who actually completed the reading assessment. AFLEARN provides a research-ready reading file constructed from the complete UNICEF source data that can be merged onto an IPUMS MICS extract. This allows you to combine the convenience of IPUMS harmonisation with complete reading data. 1.2 Why are there two routes? UNICEF releases the MICS microdata in their original survey-file structure. A MICS survey contains several data files because different questionnaires have different units of observation — for example, households, household members, women, children under five and a randomly selected child aged 5–17. We explain this structure in What’s in MICS6 data?. IPUMS MICS is a collaboration that makes MICS data easier to use across countries and survey rounds. Researchers select a unit of analysis, surveys and variables, and IPUMS provides the source data together with harmonisation syntax to create a customised extract. IPUMS is particularly useful for multi-country research because it standardises variable names, coding and documentation across surveys. See the IPUMS MICS Getting Started guide. The two approaches are therefore complementary rather than competing. 1.3 What this guide adds Neither route by itself produces the exact research-ready dataset needed for many analyses of MICS6 foundational learning. AFLEARN therefore provides additional tools for both routes. 1.3.1 If you start with UNICEF MICS The guide provides resources to: turn UNICEF’s nested download folders into a clean directory structure; merge the separate files within each country correctly; harmonise commonly used variables across MICS6 countries; and construct transparent reading variables that account for assessment language, passage length and the complex FLS reading skip patterns. Start with Organising the UNICEF download. 1.3.2 If you start with IPUMS MICS The guide provides resources to: understand the structure of an IPUMS MICS extract; and add AFLEARN’s corrected foundational reading variables constructed from the original UNICEF data. See Adding the correct reading data to an IPUMS extract. Whichever route you use, you should also read Survey design, weights and standard errors before estimating population statistics or confidence intervals. 1.4 Next steps To download the original country files, go to Getting data from UNICEF MICS. To create a harmonised multi-country extract, go to Getting data from IPUMS MICS.

2 Getting data from UNICEF MICS UNICEF is the primary source for the original MICS microdata. For work on the MICS6 Foundational Learning Skills (FLS) module, the UNICEF files are particularly important because they retain the full country-specific questionnaire structure and reading-assessment variables. This page explains how to identify and download the MICS6 surveys you need. Organising the UNICEF download then provides AFLEARN scripts to organise, merge and harmonise the downloaded files. 2.1 1. Go to the UNICEF MICS survey portal Open the UNICEF MICS surveys page. The survey catalogue can be filtered by characteristics including country, survey round and survey status. For this guide, select MICS6 as the survey round. Why MICS6? This guide deliberately focuses on MICS6 because this was the first MICS round to include the Foundational Learning Skills module. The module was administered through the Questionnaire for Children Age 5–17, with the learning assessment targeted to children aged 7–14. UNICEF’s MICS6 statistical analysis manual describes the Questionnaire for Children Age 5–17 as applying to one randomly selected child aged 5–17 in each household. Source: UNICEF, MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis. 2.2 2. Register or log in MICS microdata are available for research use through the UNICEF MICS data-access system. You may be asked to log in or register before downloading microdata. Registration and use of MICS data are free. The same approved MICS user credentials are also used when obtaining data through IPUMS MICS. See the IPUMS MICS Getting Started guidance. 2.3 3. Select the MICS6 surveys you need For each country, pay attention to the survey year, round and geographic coverage. A country may occasionally have more than one MICS dataset or a survey covering a subnational population. Do not assume that every entry labelled MICS6 represents the same geographic population. For multi-country analysis, we recommend recording at least: country; survey year; MICS round; geographic coverage; UNICEF survey/sample name; and the version of the downloaded dataset. Keeping this information with your analysis makes it much easier to reproduce the exact set of surveys used later. 2.4 4. Download the microdata and documentation UNICEF MICS downloads contain several files for each survey rather than a single rectangular analysis dataset. The exact set depends on which questionnaires and modules were administered. The files are typically distributed in SPSS (.sav) format and carry variable labels and value labels. R can read .sav files directly using packages such as haven, and Stata can import them directly. A MICS6 country download commonly includes files such as: bh.sav Birth history ch.sav Children under five fs.sav Selected child aged 5–17 hh.sav Household hl.sav Household members / household listing mn.sav Men wm.sav Women Not every survey contains every file. The exact structure depends on the questionnaires administered in that country. The file that contains the Foundational Learning Skills assessment is the fs file. However, many analyses require variables held elsewhere — for example, household characteristics from hh or information about household members from hl. This is why understanding the file structure and merging rules is important. We cover these in Files, units of observation and identifiers. 2.5 Download the survey documentation too Do not download only the microdata. The country documentation is essential for interpreting the variables correctly. Where available, retain: the survey report; questionnaires; interviewer instructions or enumeration materials; sampling documentation; dataset readme files; and any country-specific notes supplied with the release. This is especially important for the FLS reading assessment because countries could adapt the language and wording of the reading materials. The generic MICS6 questionnaire documentation itself notes that countries may differ in the exact words, names and stories used in the reading passage. See the IPUMS rendering of the standard MICS6 Questionnaire for Children Age 5–17. For reading analyses, keep the country questionnaires and reading materials You will need to know which reading passage a child attempted and how long that passage was in order to construct reading accuracy correctly. These details cannot always be recovered from the released analysis variables alone. AFLEARN has compiled the required assessment-language and passage-length information for the surveys supported by this guide. See Constructing research-ready reading variables. 2.6 5. Messy nested survey archives If you download several surveys together, the resulting archive can contain multiple nested folders and zip files. The data are all there, but the folder structure is inconvenient for reproducible analysis. For example, after manually unzipping a bulk download you may encounter something like: MICS_Datasets.zip └── country folder └── another archive └── another folder ├── fs.sav ├── hh.sav ├── hl.sav └── ... There is no analytical reason to retain this nesting. AFLEARN provides an R script, prepare-mics-fs.R, that turns the bulk UNICEF download into a simple structure with one directory per survey: Data/UNICEF/ ├── BEN_2021_MICS6_v01_M/ │ ├── bh.sav │ ├── ch.sav │ ├── fs.sav │ ├── hh.sav │ ├── hl.sav │ ├── wm.sav │ └── ... ├── GHA_2017_MICS6_v01_M/ │ └── ... └── ... You do not need to reorganise these folders manually. The script and instructions are provided in Organising the UNICEF download. 2.7 When should I use the UNICEF files? The UNICEF route is the best choice when: you need variables that have not been harmonised by IPUMS; you want to understand or reproduce country-specific MICS measures; you are working directly with item-level FLS data; you need the complete foundational reading information; or you want full control over how variables are harmonised across surveys. For many multi-country projects, a useful strategy is to use IPUMS for harmonised background variables and UNICEF source files for foundational reading. AFLEARN provides the tools to combine the two. 2.8 Next step Before processing the files, read What’s in MICS6 data?. It explains why MICS data are split across files, what the different units of observation are, and how the fs file relates to the household and household-member files. If you are already familiar with the MICS file structure, continue directly to Organising the UNICEF download.

3 Getting data from IPUMS MICS IPUMS MICS provides a powerful way to work with MICS data across countries. Rather than downloading every variable from every original survey file and harmonising them yourself, you select the unit of analysis, surveys and variables you need. IPUMS then supplies the original UNICEF source data together with syntax that harmonises your selections and builds a pooled extract. For many multi-country analyses, this substantially reduces the amount of data preparation required. However, there is an important exception for the MICS6 foundational reading assessment. If your research uses reading outcomes, read A critical limitation for foundational reading below before deciding which variables to extract. 3.1 What does IPUMS MICS do? MICS questionnaires and variable coding can differ across countries and survey rounds. IPUMS MICS creates harmonised variables that make comparable concepts easier to identify and analyse across surveys. The IPUMS system also provides detailed variable-level documentation, including: variable definitions; codes and labels; the surveys in which a variable is available; the universe — the population for whom a question was asked or a variable is defined; questionnaire text; and links to survey-specific source documentation. This documentation is one of the major advantages of using IPUMS. IPUMS explicitly warns that researchers can make incorrect comparisons if they fail to account for differences in variable universes across MICS surveys. See the IPUMS MICS FAQ. 3.2 1. Register as a MICS user You must be an approved UNICEF MICS data user to download an IPUMS MICS extract. IPUMS states that the same UNICEF MICS login credentials are used to access IPUMS MICS data. Registration and use are free. See Getting Started with IPUMS MICS. 3.3 2. Choose your unit of analysis From GET DATA, IPUMS asks you to choose a unit of analysis. Available units include: women; children under five; children aged 5–17; births; men; household members; and household characteristics. For analyses of the MICS6 Foundational Learning Skills module, your main unit of analysis will usually be children aged 5–17. One extract has one unit of analysis IPUMS MICS allows a single unit of analysis within an extract. If you need information from another unit — for example, household or parent characteristics — some variables may already have been attached or harmonised for your chosen unit, while other analyses may require linking files. IPUMS provides separate guidance on linking units of analysis. 3.4 3. Select MICS6 samples Use the sample-selection interface to choose the MICS6 surveys required for your analysis. For a multi-country foundational-learning project, we recommend keeping a record of the exact IPUMS sample identifiers used. These sample identifiers are preferable to relying only on country names because they identify the specific survey and year. 3.5 4. Select variables You can browse variables by topic or search for particular concepts and add them to your Data Cart. Before adding a variable, inspect its documentation. In particular, check: whether it is available in all the MICS6 surveys you plan to use; whether its meaning is comparable across those samples; whether response categories have been harmonised; the variable’s universe; and any survey-specific comparability notes. Some identifying and technical variables are added to IPUMS extracts automatically. We recommend retaining the identifiers and sample variables required to link records and to set up the survey design, even if you do not expect to use them immediately. 3.6 5. Create the extract Once you have selected your samples and variables, open the Data Cart and choose CREATE DATA EXTRACT. IPUMS MICS differs from some other IPUMS products in how the final harmonised file is produced. According to the current IPUMS instructions, the download contains the source data and Stata syntax. You run the supplied main .do file, which applies the IPUMS harmonisation and creates the pooled dataset. See IPUMS MICS: General Instructions for Opening an Extract. Because the extract-building step runs Stata syntax, an R workflow needs Stata once to create the harmonised file; the saved file can then be read and analysed in R. 3.7 A critical problem with the IPUMS foundational reading data The IPUMS MICS reading variables should not be used for a MICS6 survey that administered more than one reading passage. In these surveys, IPUMS retains data for only one of the passages. Children assessed using another passage therefore appear to have no data on the harmonised reading variables. This is not ordinary item non-response: it systematically excludes children according to the language/passage in which they were assessed and can make estimates of reading performance seriously misleading. This issue is especially important in multilingual African countries. MICS6 allowed countries to adapt the reading assessment to local languages. The country-specific source files can therefore contain separate variables for different passages or languages, while the corresponding IPUMS harmonised reading variable represents only one of them. 3.7.1 Malawi illustrates the problem clearly The Malawi MICS 2019–20 administered the reading assessment in both English and Chichewa. The original Malawi questionnaire contains separate English and Chichewa reading pathways, including separate results variables. UNICEF’s Malawi reporting also explicitly states that the foundational reading assessment was conducted in English and Chichewa. The consequences of using the IPUMS reading variables are substantial: Malawi MICS 2019–20 Number of children Have FLWORDSATTEMPT in the IPUMS extract (English passage) 1,720 Attempted the Chichewa passage in the original UNICEF data 3,970 Attempted both passages 130 The original UNICEF source data confirm 3,970 valid observations for FLB20A, the number of words attempted in the Chichewa passage. The Malawi questionnaire documentation also shows separate FL20 and FL20B reading-results fields, with FL20B corresponding to the Chichewa passage. The implication is important. Most children who attempted the Chichewa passage have no corresponding value in the IPUMS FLWORDSATTEMPT variable. An analysis that treated the IPUMS variable as the Malawi reading sample would therefore omit the Chichewa assessment data and could give a badly distorted picture of reading performance. This is not a minor loss of information that can be addressed by dropping a few missing observations. It changes who is represented in the reading analysis. The problem is not that IPUMS has miscoded the retained passage; it is that the other passage or passages are absent. This limitation is specific to the harmonised foundational-reading variables in multi-passage surveys — for everything outside the reading assessment, IPUMS harmonisation remains extremely useful. 3.7.2 AFLEARN’s solution AFLEARN reconstructs the reading data from the original UNICEF MICS6 country files, retaining all relevant passages and languages. We provide an R script, harmonize-mics-reading-v1.1.R, that harmonises the child-level foundational-reading variables directly from those files. It constructs research-ready variables using: the child’s assessment language; the correct passage length for that assessment; the number of words attempted; the number of words read incorrectly or missed; the reading comprehension items; and the MICS6 reading skip patterns. The resulting file also includes identifiers that allow these variables to be merged onto an IPUMS MICS child extract. This means that researchers can use: IPUMS MICS for harmonised demographic, household, schooling and other background variables + AFLEARN reading file constructed from the original UNICEF MICS data for complete and correctly constructed foundational reading outcomes. The step-by-step merge instructions are in Adding the correct reading data to an IPUMS extract. The reading limitation is therefore a reason to supplement IPUMS, not a reason to avoid it. 3.8 Next steps Before building an extract, read What’s in MICS6 data? to understand the MICS survey structure and the FLS module. If you already have an IPUMS extract, continue to Adding the correct reading data to an IPUMS extract.

4 What’s in MICS6 data? 4.1 The key idea: MICS links information across levels

4 What’s in MICS6 data? Before analysing MICS6 foundational learning data, it is important to understand how a MICS survey is organised. MICS is not a school assessment dataset and it is not delivered as one flat file. It is a household survey containing several questionnaires and data files with different units of observation. This section explains: how MICS6 is structured; which files are relevant for research on children and learning; how households and individuals are identified across files; how children enter the fs file; what the Foundational Learning Skills (FLS) module measures; and why the reading data require particular care. Why this matters Many errors in MICS analysis happen before a statistical model is run. Using the wrong file, misunderstanding who appears in the fs dataset, merging on an incomplete identifier, or treating a reading skip as ordinary missing data can all change the population represented in an analysis. The UNICEF MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis is the main reference for the MICS6 questionnaire structure and standard indicator construction. The UNICEF Foundational Learning Skills Module resource provides additional background on the learning assessment. 4.1 The key idea: MICS links information across levels A useful way to think about MICS is as a set of linked datasets: HOUSEHOLD │ ├── household characteristics │ ├── household member 1 ├── household member 2 ├── household member 3 │ │ │ ├── may have an individual questionnaire │ │ │ └── may be selected for the 5–17 questionnaire │ └── household member n The household questionnaire tells us about the household and everyone listed in it. Additional questionnaires collect more detailed information for particular populations, including women, men, children under five and one randomly selected child aged 5–17 per household. For foundational-learning research, the most important files are usually: fs: the selected child aged 5–17; hl: all household members; and hh: the household. Researchers may also need other files for particular questions. The next page explains these files and their identifiers in detail: Files, units of observation and identifiers.

5 Files, units of observation and identifiers 5.1 Why does MICS have separate files? MICS6 is built from several questionnaires. Different questionnaires collect information about different populations, so the resulting datasets have different units of observation. For example, a household has one record in the household file, but every person listed in that household has a separate record in the household-member file. One randomly selected child aged 5–17 may then have a further record in the fs file. UNICEF’s MICS6 statistical analysis manual describes five core questionnaire groups: Household Questionnaire; Questionnaire for Individual Women aged 15–49; Questionnaire for Individual Men aged 15–49; Questionnaire for Children Under Five; and Questionnaire for Children aged 5–17, administered for one randomly selected child aged 5–17 in each household. See the MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis. 5.2 Common MICS6 data files The exact files available can vary with the questionnaires and modules implemented in a country. The following are the files researchers are most likely to encounter. File Unit of observation Examples of information hh Household Household characteristics, wealth-related variables, water and sanitation, household-level identifiers hl Household member Age, sex, relationship to household head, education and other roster information for household members wm Woman aged 15–49 Women’s individual questionnaire mn Man aged 15–49, where administered Men’s individual questionnaire ch Child under five Information collected through the under-five questionnaire fs One randomly selected child aged 5–17 per sampled household Child background, schooling, child labour, child functioning, parental involvement and the Foundational Learning Skills module bh Birth Birth-history records derived from women’s questionnaire data For foundational learning The FLS assessment is in the fs file. However, that does not mean everything you need for an analysis is in fs. Household and household-member characteristics often need to be added from hh and hl. 5.3 The hh file: one record per household The household file contains information that applies at household level. The core household identifier is: HH1 = cluster number HH2 = household number Within a survey, the combination of HH1 and HH2 identifies the sampled household. Conceptually: HH1 HH2 household 101 01 household A 101 02 household B 102 01 household C If you merge household-level information onto an individual-level file, every individual from the same household receives the same household information. 5.4 The hl file: one record per household member The household listing contains one record for each person listed as a member of the household. It therefore needs one additional identifier: HH1 + HH2 + HL1 where: HH1 identifies the cluster; HH2 identifies the household within the cluster; and HL1 is the household member’s line number. For example: HH1 HH2 HL1 101 01 1 101 01 2 101 01 3 101 02 1 The first three observations are three different people in the same household. A line number is only unique within a household HL1 = 2 does not identify a person by itself. Many households have a member on line 2. An individual must be identified using the household identifiers and the line number. 5.5 The fs file: one selected child per household The fs dataset contains the Questionnaire for Children Age 5–17. Important identifiers include: HH1 cluster HH2 household LN selected child's household line number The standard MICS6 questionnaire records the selected child’s name and household line number in FS3. Released datasets commonly also provide that line number as LN. The selected child can therefore be linked back to their own record in the household listing: fs: HH1 + HH2 + LN │ │ LN corresponds to HL1 ▼ hl: HH1 + HH2 + HL1 This is the basis for adding household-roster information about the selected child. 5.6 Household links versus person links This distinction is fundamental. 5.6.1 Linking fs to hh If you want a household characteristic, you link using: HH1 + HH2 For example: household wealth; household location; water and sanitation; household size; or another household-level characteristic. 5.6.2 Linking the selected child in fs to their own hl record If you want information about that child from the household roster, you link: fs: HH1 + HH2 + LN hl: HH1 + HH2 + HL1 For example, you may want to check or add information recorded for the child in the household questionnaire. 5.6.3 Linking the child to another person Some variables in the child questionnaire contain the household line number of another household member. For example, FS4 records the line number of the child’s mother or caretaker in the standard MICS6 questionnaire. This is a different type of link: selected child HH1 + HH2 + FS4 │ │ FS4 identifies another household member ▼ household listing HH1 + HH2 + HL1 If that person is also eligible for another individual questionnaire, their line number can potentially be used to link to that questionnaire as well. Same household does not mean same person A merge on HH1 + HH2 attaches household-level information. A merge on HH1 + HH2 + line number identifies a particular person. These are analytically different operations. We provide tested R and Stata code for these common links in Merging MICS6 files within a country. 5.7 A visual map of the files used most often in learning research HOUSEHOLD hh HH1 + HH2 │ ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ HOUSEHOLD MEMBERS SELECTED CHILD hl fs HH1 + HH2 + HL1 HH1 + HH2 + LN ▲ │ │ │ └──────── LN = HL1 ──────────┘ child's own roster record SELECTED CHILD HOUSEHOLD MEMBER fs hl HH1 + HH2 + FS4 ─────────────► HH1 + HH2 + HL1 mother/caretaker link 5.8 Do not merge files until you know the unit of analysis Suppose your research question is: What proportion of children aged 10 have foundational numeracy skills, by household wealth? Your unit of analysis is the selected child, so fs should remain the analysis file. You add the household characteristic to those child records. You should not turn the household file into the analysis population simply because the wealth variable comes from hh. This distinction also determines which survey weight you use. We return to this in Survey design, weights and standard errors. 5.9 Variable names can differ The names above reflect the standard MICS6 structure, but country datasets can contain adaptations and additional variables. Always consult: the country questionnaire; variable and value labels in the released dataset; and country-specific documentation. AFLEARN’s harmonisation scripts deal with many of the cross-country differences relevant to foundational-learning research. See Harmonising variables across countries.

6 Who is in the fs file? Understanding the fs sample is essential before analysing the Foundational Learning Skills data. The fs file is sometimes loosely described as the “children aged 5–17 file”. That is useful shorthand, but it can obscure two important facts: only one eligible child aged 5–17 is randomly selected per sampled household for the questionnaire; and the Foundational Learning Skills assessment itself targets children aged 7–14, not everyone in the fs file. UNICEF documents the 5–17 questionnaire as being administered for one randomly selected child aged 5–17 in each household. The standard questionnaire then routes children aged 5–6 and 15–17 around the FLS module, leaving children aged 7–14 eligible for the learning assessment. See the MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis and standard MICS6 Questionnaire for Children Age 5–17. 6.1 From household members to the FLS sample Conceptually, the process is: Sampled household │ ▼ List all household members │ ▼ Identify children aged 5–17 │ ▼ Randomly select one eligible child │ ▼ Create an fs questionnaire/record │ ├──────── age 5–6 ────────► no FLS assessment │ ├──────── age 7–14 ───────► eligible for FLS assessment │ └──────── age 15–17 ──────► no FLS assessment This has several implications for analysis. 6.2 The fs file is not a census of all children aged 5–17 in sampled households A household can contain more than one child aged 5–17, but only one is selected for the questionnaire. For example: Household A child age 8 ┐ child age 11 ├── one randomly selected for fs child age 16 ┘ You therefore cannot simply merge the fs file onto every child aged 5–17 in hl and treat the result as if all children had been assessed. The selection process is reflected in the survey weight for the 5–17 questionnaire. 6.3 Use the fs weight for analyses whose observations are selected children MICS provides questionnaire-specific survey weights. For the selected child file, the standard weight is fsweight. If your outcome is foundational reading or numeracy and your analysis dataset consists of fs records, the relevant weight is the fs weight, even if you merge household or household-member characteristics onto those records. For example: Outcome: foundational numeracy from fs Age: child age from fs/hl Wealth quintile: from hh Unit of analysis: selected child Weight: fsweight The source of a covariate does not determine the survey weight. The analysis population does. We explain weights, clustering and stratification in detail in Survey design, weights and standard errors. 6.4 The FLS target population is children aged 7–14 The MICS6 FLS module directly assesses reading and numeracy among children aged 7–14. UNICEF describes the module as measuring skills expected at approximately Grade 2/3 level in a household-survey setting. This age range is one of the major analytical strengths of MICS. Researchers can examine foundational skills: among children currently attending school; among children who have never attended school; among children who attended previously but are no longer in school; by age rather than only grade; across grades; and in relation to household and family characteristics. Because MICS is household based, the assessment is not restricted to children who are present in school on an assessment day. 6.5 Being age 7–14 does not guarantee a completed assessment Age determines eligibility for the FLS module, but not every eligible child necessarily completes every assessment task. The reading module contains several routing decisions. A child may, for example: not receive permission to participate; not assent to participate; be routed away from the reading passage because an appropriate assessment language is unavailable; decline to read; not progress through the practice items where these apply; or begin the assessment but not complete it. These cases should not automatically be treated as equivalent missing values. This is one reason AFLEARN constructs a reading_status variable that makes the reading pathway explicit. We introduce the assessment sequence in Understanding the MICS6 reading assessment and provide the research-ready construction in Constructing MICS6 reading outcomes. 6.6 Age, grade and the official indicators are different concepts MICS allows researchers to describe foundational learning for several populations. For example, UNICEF tabulations distinguish between: children aged 7–14; children of the expected age for Grade 2/3; and children actually attending Grade 2/3. These denominators answer different questions. A child aged 10 in Grade 2 can contribute to a grade-based Grade 2/3 estimate even though they are older than the expected age for that grade. Conversely, a child of the expected Grade 2/3 age may be in a different grade or out of school. Always state your denominator “Percentage with foundational reading skills” is incomplete unless the reader knows among whom: all children aged 7–14, children of Grade 2/3 age, children attending Grade 2/3, or another explicitly defined population. This guide’s worked examples will show how to construct and report these populations transparently.

7 The Foundational Learning Skills module The Foundational Learning Skills (FLS) module was introduced in MICS6 to directly assess basic reading and numeracy skills through a household survey. UNICEF describes the module as assessing skills expected in the early primary grades, with children aged 7–14 as the target population. Because the assessment is administered in households rather than schools, it includes children regardless of whether they are currently enrolled or attending school. See UNICEF’s Foundational Learning Skills Module and the MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis. 7.1 What does the module assess? The module contains two broad assessment areas: FOUNDATIONAL LEARNING SKILLS │ ├── READING │ ├── oral reading accuracy │ ├── literal comprehension │ └── inferential comprehension │ └── NUMERACY ├── number reading ├── number discrimination ├── addition └── pattern recognition The released microdata contain substantially more information than a single “meets/does not meet” indicator. Researchers can work with the underlying tasks and items to examine where in the progression children are succeeding or struggling. Do not restrict yourself automatically to the headline indicator The official binary foundational-skills indicators are useful for reporting a common benchmark, but they discard substantial information. The item-level data allow analysis of individual domains, total scores, patterns of mastery and distributions of performance. 7.2 The assessment is not a conventional school test The FLS module differs from many international and national learning assessments in several ways. It is: administered in the child’s household; administered to a broad age range rather than one school grade; able to include children who are out of school; relatively short; designed around foundational skills expected in early primary school; and embedded within a much larger household survey. This creates important research opportunities. Learning can be studied alongside household wealth, family composition, disability, schooling histories and other characteristics collected in MICS. It also creates comparability issues that researchers need to consider, particularly: children’s age and grade; whether they are currently in school; the timing of fieldwork within the school year; and the language in which reading was assessed. Later worked examples show how these features can be incorporated into analysis. 7.3 Official foundational reading skills UNICEF defines foundational reading skills using three components: oral reading accuracy — the child reads at least 90% of the words in the story correctly; literal comprehension — the child answers all three literal comprehension questions correctly; and inferential comprehension — the child answers both inferential comprehension questions correctly. A child must satisfy all three to be classified as having foundational reading skills. This is a demanding conjunctive indicator: failure to meet any one component means the child does not meet the overall benchmark. The reading assessment is explained in detail in Understanding the MICS6 reading assessment. 7.4 Official foundational numeracy skills UNICEF defines four numeracy tasks: number reading — 6 items; number discrimination — 5 items; addition — 5 items; and pattern recognition and completion — 5 items. To successfully complete a task, the child must answer all items within that task correctly. To be classified as having foundational numeracy skills, the child must successfully complete all four tasks. The UNICEF FLS adaptation guidelines set out these rules in the standard tabulation plan. We describe the item structure in Understanding the MICS6 numeracy assessment. 7.5 FLS and SDG 4.1.1(a) The MICS6 FLS module was developed to contribute information on foundational reading and numeracy at the Grade 2/3 level. MICS tabulation plans report indicators for children attending Grade 2/3 and for children of the expected age for Grade 2/3, as well as broader age-based tabulations. When using MICS for cross-country research, it is useful to distinguish: the assessment tasks; the MICS foundational-skills definitions; and the population used for a particular indicator. These are related, but they are not the same thing. 7.6 Next Reading has additional complications involving language, passage selection, practice items and skip patterns. Continue to Understanding the MICS6 reading assessment.

8 Understanding the MICS6 reading assessment Reading is the most complex part of the MICS6 Foundational Learning Skills data. At first glance the assessment appears straightforward: a child reads a story and answers comprehension questions. In the microdata, however, several earlier decisions determine whether the child reaches the story, which story they receive, and how their subsequent data should be interpreted. Understanding this sequence is essential before constructing reading outcomes. 8.1 Overview of the reading assessment At a high level, the assessment involves: Eligible child age 7–14 │ ▼ Permission / child participation │ ▼ Determine assessment language │ ▼ Does the child agree to read? │ ▼ Practice / routing where applicable │ ▼ Read story │ ├── words attempted ├── words missed / read incorrectly │ ▼ Comprehension questions │ ├── 3 literal └── 2 inferential The exact country questionnaire should always be consulted because language options and country adaptations differ. 8.2 Assessment language is part of the data-generating process The standard MICS6 questionnaire asks about the language the child speaks at home and, for children with schooling experience, the language used by teachers. The questionnaire then uses this information to determine whether an appropriate reading booklet is available and which language should be used for the reading task. In the standard questionnaire: FL7 records the language spoken most of the time at home; FL9A/FL9B asks about the language used by teachers for children with schooling experience; and the subsequent reading instructions route the child to an available reading booklet/language. This means that reading performance cannot always be separated from assessment-language availability and assignment. In multilingual surveys, countries may have more than one reading passage. As discussed in Getting data from IPUMS MICS, this is also why the IPUMS reading variables are unsafe to use for multi-passage countries. 8.3 Not every eligible child attempts the story There are several reasons an age-eligible child may have no story-reading result. For example: age 7–14 │ ├── permission not given ├── child does not participate ├── suitable assessment language unavailable ├── child declines reading ├── routed out through practice sequence └── attempts main story These pathways do not all have the same substantive meaning. A child who was never offered an appropriate passage because of language availability is different from a child who attempted a passage but could not read it. Treating both simply as NA obscures that distinction. This is why AFLEARN constructs a research-ready reading-status variable. The variable records whether the child reached the reading task and, where they did not, the reason for the missing reading result. The construction is provided in Constructing MICS6 reading outcomes. 8.4 Practice items and routing The standard MICS6 reading sequence contains practice/routing items before the main story for some children. The routing depends partly on age and schooling experience. Researchers should therefore not infer inability to read simply because the main story variables are missing. The correct interpretation requires following the questionnaire skip pattern. AFLEARN’s processing script does this explicitly rather than relying on missingness in the final story variables. 8.5 Oral reading accuracy For children who attempt the main story, the interviewer records reading performance. The official foundational-reading definition requires the child to read at least 90% of the story words correctly. Conceptually: words read correctly -------------------- >= 0.90 total story words The difficulty is that the denominator — total story words — is not provided as a simple analysis variable in all released country datasets. Moreover, story length can vary with country and language adaptation. You cannot calculate the 90% accuracy criterion correctly without the passage length Counting only the child’s attempted or incorrect words is insufficient unless you also know how many words were in the passage the child received. AFLEARN therefore created a passage-length variable from the country assessment materials and an assessment-language variable identifying the relevant passage. These are used in the research-ready reading construction in Section 3. 8.6 Literal comprehension Children who progress through the reading task are asked three literal comprehension questions. Literal questions ask about information stated directly in the story. Under the MICS foundational-reading definition, the child must answer all three correctly to satisfy the literal-comprehension component. 8.7 Inferential comprehension Children are also asked two inferential comprehension questions. These require the child to draw meaning from information that is implied rather than simply repeat a stated fact. The child must answer both correctly to satisfy the inferential-comprehension component. 8.8 The overall foundational reading indicator The official MICS definition combines all three components: READING ACCURACY >= 90% of story words correct │ AND │ 3/3 LITERAL QUESTIONS CORRECT │ AND │ 2/2 INFERENTIAL QUESTIONS CORRECT │ ▼ FOUNDATIONAL READING SKILLS UNICEF’s MICS6 statistical analysis manual describes this as a conjunctive indicator: the child must satisfy the accuracy, literal-comprehension and inferential-comprehension requirements. 8.9 Why the raw reading variables are not enough for our purposes For multi-country analysis, researchers face three related problems. 8.9.1 1. Passage length The released datasets do not provide a single harmonised variable giving the number of words in the passage administered to each child. 8.9.2 2. Assessment language and passage Countries with more than one reading language can have multiple sets of passage variables. Researchers need to identify which passage the child actually attempted. 8.9.3 3. Complex skip patterns A blank story result can arise for different reasons. Without reconstructing the questionnaire pathway, it is easy to classify children incorrectly or silently change the analysis sample. AFLEARN’s research-ready variables address all three problems. 8.10 What AFLEARN adds The Section 3 processing produces variables that make the reading data easier to analyse transparently, including: assessment language; passage length; reading status; reading accuracy measures; literal-comprehension measures; inferential-comprehension measures; and an overall foundational-reading indicator. The detailed harmonisation and country-specific derivations will be documented separately in the technical appendix. Most users of this guide do not need to reproduce that work; they need to understand what the derived variables mean and how to use them correctly. 8.11 A note on cross-country comparisons Reading comparisons deserve more caution than numeracy comparisons because reading is inherently language dependent. Differences across countries may reflect not only underlying reading skill but also features such as: language of instruction; language spoken at home; language in which the child was assessed; linguistic characteristics of the assessment language; country adaptation of the story; and the relationship between the assessment language and the child’s schooling experience. The MICS6 assessment was designed for national monitoring and uses country/language adaptation. Researchers should therefore avoid interpreting a difference in raw reading performance across countries as if every child completed an identical language-neutral test. These issues do not make cross-country analysis impossible, but they should shape the research question and interpretation. 8.12 Next The numeracy assessment has a simpler common structure. See Understanding the MICS6 numeracy assessment.

9 Understanding the MICS6 numeracy assessment The MICS6 foundational numeracy assessment consists of 21 items organised into four tasks. Unlike reading, the numeracy assessment does not involve language-specific passages of different lengths. This makes the data considerably simpler to prepare for multi-country analysis, although researchers should still examine country questionnaires and routing. UNICEF describes the four domains as number reading, number discrimination, addition, and pattern recognition. 9.1 Structure of the assessment Task Number of items What the child does Number reading 6 Reads numbers shown by the interviewer Number discrimination 5 Identifies the larger of two numbers Addition 5 Solves addition problems Pattern recognition and completion 5 Identifies the missing number in a sequence Total 21 The standard MICS6 booklet moves from relatively simple items to more demanding ones within the assessment. 9.2 1. Number reading The child is shown six numbers and asked to identify each one. The standard assessment includes numbers ranging from one to three digits. The official MICS task indicator requires the child to answer all six items correctly. 9.3 2. Number discrimination The child is shown five pairs of numbers and asked to identify which number in each pair is larger. The official task indicator requires all five items correct. 9.4 3. Addition The child is given five addition problems. These include simple single-digit calculations and more demanding items. Again, successful completion of the MICS addition task requires all five items correct. 9.5 4. Pattern recognition and completion The child is shown five number sequences with a missing value and asked to supply the missing number. The official task indicator requires all five items correct. 9.6 Foundational numeracy requires mastery of all four tasks The official MICS6 definition is deliberately stringent: 6/6 number-reading items AND 5/5 number-discrimination items AND 5/5 addition items AND 5/5 pattern items │ ▼ FOUNDATIONAL NUMERACY SKILLS UNICEF’s standard tabulation plan specifies that a child must correctly complete every item within each task and all four tasks to demonstrate foundational numeracy skills. See the UNICEF FLS module adaptation guidelines. 9.7 The binary indicator hides a lot of information Because the official measure requires success on every task, children with very different skill profiles can receive the same value. For example: Number Discrim. Addition Pattern Total Child A 6/6 5/5 5/5 4/5 20/21 Child B 3/6 1/5 0/5 0/5 4/21 Foundational numeracy? NO — — — NO Both are classified as not demonstrating foundational numeracy skills, but their observed performance is clearly very different. For research purposes, it is often informative to examine: each of the four task indicators; the individual items; number of items correct within each task; total items correct out of 21; and the overall foundational-numeracy indicator. Which measure is appropriate depends on the research question. 9.8 Stop rules and non-attempts The standard questionnaire includes interviewer instructions and stop rules within parts of the numeracy assessment. Item responses can therefore distinguish correct, incorrect and no-attempt outcomes. When constructing scores, researchers should not automatically treat every blank or non-attempt as equivalent without checking the questionnaire routing. The worked examples later in this guide show how AFLEARN constructs transparent numeracy scores from the item-level data. 9.9 Comparing numeracy across countries Numeracy avoids some of the language-specific complications of reading, but comparison still requires care. In particular, researchers should consider: age; grade; whether the child is currently attending school; exposure to schooling within the current year; survey timing; and differences in schooling systems. A Grade 3 child assessed near the beginning of a school year has had less exposure to Grade 3 instruction than a Grade 3 child assessed near the end of the year. This matters when interpreting apparent cross-country differences. 9.10 Headline indicators and distributions answer different questions The MICS foundational-numeracy indicator answers: What proportion of children demonstrate mastery of all four specified foundational numeracy tasks? A total score answers a different question: How many of the 21 observed numeracy items can children answer correctly? Neither is universally preferable. The important point is to choose the measure that matches the research question and describe it accurately. The worked examples in Section 6 use both approaches.

10 Organising the UNICEF download When several MICS surveys are downloaded together, UNICEF packages them in a bulk zip containing survey folders, further archives and wrapper directories. The data are usable, but manually unpacking many surveys is tedious and creates opportunities for path and naming errors. AFLEARN provides an R script, prepare-mics-fs.R, to do this automatically. 10.1 What the script does The script prepare-mics-fs.R: creates the working folders used throughout this guide; finds the UNICEF MICS_Datasets.zip; extracts the nested archives; retains the survey .sav files and readme documentation; removes unnecessary wrapper folders; creates one clean folder for each survey; and copies itself, and any AFLEARN harmonisation scripts it finds alongside the zip, into Script/. It uses base R only, so no packages need to be installed first. 10.2 Before A bulk UNICEF download may look conceptually like this: MICS_Datasets.zip └── survey folder └── another archive └── wrapper folder ├── fs.sav ├── hh.sav ├── hl.sav └── ... 10.3 After AFLEARN’s script produces: Data/ ├── UNICEF/ │ ├── BEN_2021_MICS6_v01_M/ │ │ ├── bh.sav │ │ ├── ch.sav │ │ ├── fs.sav │ │ ├── hh.sav │ │ ├── hl.sav │ │ ├── wm.sav │ │ └── ... │ ├── GHA_2017_MICS6_v01_M/ │ │ └── ... │ └── ... ├── IPUMS/ └── AFLEARN Harmonised Data/ Script/ └── prepare-mics-fs.R The three folders under Data/ separate the three kinds of data this guide uses: Folder Contents Data/UNICEF/ The original country files, one folder per survey, written by this script Data/IPUMS/ Your own IPUMS MICS extracts. Created empty; see Getting data from IPUMS MICS Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/ Created empty. The harmonisation scripts write their output here Script/ sits alongside Data/ and holds every R and Stata script you run. Each survey therefore has a predictable path such as: Data/UNICEF/BEN_2021_MICS6_v01_M/fs.sav That predictable structure is what the later harmonisation scripts expect. 10.4 How to run it Download prepare-mics-fs.R from the AFLEARN MICS6-Guide repository and place it next to MICS_Datasets.zip. Then, in R: setwd("C:/path/to/folder/with/zip/and/script") source("prepare-mics-fs.R") Sourcing the script runs it. It creates Data/UNICEF/, Data/IPUMS/, Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/ and Script/ under that folder, then fills in the UNICEF survey folders. Running it again is safe: folders that already exist are left alone. If you are working inside the MICS6-Guide project, the script finds the project root and builds the same structure there, whichever subfolder you run it from. The original bulk zip is retained by default. If you deliberately want to delete it after successful extraction: prepare_mics_data(remove_zip = TRUE) If the zip is somewhere else: source("prepare-mics-fs.R") prepare_mics_data( zip = "C:/path/to/MICS_Datasets.zip" ) 10.5 Check the result Before continuing, check that R can see the survey folders and files: dir.exists("Data/UNICEF") list.files("Data/UNICEF") file.exists( "Data/UNICEF/BEN_2021_MICS6_v01_M/fs.sav" ) You can also confirm that R can open one of the SPSS files: library(haven) fs <- read_sav( "Data/UNICEF/BEN_2021_MICS6_v01_M/fs.sav" ) dim(fs) Keep the original download We recommend keeping the original UNICEF zip in a separate raw-data location, even if you use AFLEARN’s clean folder structure for analysis. Raw source data should remain unchanged so that the preparation process is reproducible. 10.6 Next If you need variables from more than one MICS file within a country, continue to Merging MICS6 files within a country. If all the variables you need are already in fs, you can move directly to Harmonising variables across countries.

11 Merging MICS6 files within a country MICS data are split across files because the files have different units of observation. You will often need to add information from another file to the selected-child (fs) data. The most important rule is: Decide what one row of your final dataset represents before you merge anything. For foundational-learning research, one row will usually represent the selected child in fs. The safest workflow is therefore generally to start with fs and add the variables you need. UNICEF’s MICS6 statistical analysis manual includes specific guidance on merging MICS datasets and describes the identifiers used across questionnaire files. See the MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis. 11.1 Three common types of link 11.1.1 1. Add household information to the selected child Use: HH1 + HH2 Conceptually: fs child hh household HH1 HH2 LN HH1 HH2 101 01 3 ───────────────► 101 01 This is appropriate for variables that genuinely have one value per household. 11.1.2 2. Add the selected child’s own household-list information Use: fs: HH1 + HH2 + LN hl: HH1 + HH2 + HL1 where the selected child’s LN corresponds to their HL1 in the household listing. 11.1.3 3. Link the child to another household member Some questionnaire variables store another person’s household line number. For example, FS4 identifies the child’s mother/caretaker in the standard MICS6 questionnaire. In that case the key is: HH1 + HH2 + other person's line number not the child’s own LN. See Files, units of observation and identifiers for the conceptual explanation.

12 Example 1: add household variables to fs Suppose we want to add household variables from hh.sav. 12.1 R library(haven) library(dplyr) fs <- read_sav("Data/UNICEF/COUNTRY_SURVEY/fs.sav") hh <- read_sav("Data/UNICEF/COUNTRY_SURVEY/hh.sav") # Check that there is only one household record per key hh %>% count(HH1, HH2) %>% filter(n > 1) # Keep only the household variables needed hh_keep <- hh %>% select(HH1, HH2, variable_1, variable_2) # Add them to the selected-child records fs_merged <- fs %>% left_join( hh_keep, by = c("HH1", "HH2"), relationship = "many-to-one" ) Replace variable_1 and variable_2 with the variables required for your analysis. Using relationship = "many-to-one" makes your expectation explicit: many child/individual records may refer to a household, but there should be only one matching household record for each HH1 + HH2 key. 12.2 Stata use "Data/UNICEF/COUNTRY_SURVEY/fs.dta", clear merge m:1 HH1 HH2 using /// "Data/UNICEF/COUNTRY_SURVEY/hh.dta", /// keepusing(variable_1 variable_2) tab _merge If you are working directly with UNICEF’s .sav files in Stata, import the SPSS files first and save temporary .dta versions.

14 Always validate a merge 14.1 R checks 14.2 Stata checks

14 Always validate a merge Do not regard a merge command completing without an error as evidence that the merge is correct. Before merging, ask: What does one row represent in each file? Should the key be unique in one file or both? Are the line numbers identifying the same person? How many rows should the analysis dataset have after the merge? Then inspect the result. 14.1 R checks # Number of rows should normally remain the same as fs nrow(fs) nrow(fs_merged) # Child identifier should remain unique fs_merged %>% count(HH1, HH2, LN) %>% filter(n > 1) For important merges, use an indicator to identify unmatched observations rather than silently accepting them. fs_check <- fs %>% left_join( hl %>% select(HH1, HH2, HL1, variable_1), by = c("HH1", "HH2", "LN" = "HL1"), relationship = "one-to-one", unmatched = "drop" ) For production work, we recommend explicitly counting unmatched records rather than simply dropping them. 14.2 Stata checks Stata creates _merge automatically: tab _merge Interpret: 1 = record only in master 2 = record only in using file 3 = matched Do not automatically write: drop if _merge != 3 until you understand why observations did not match.

Differences can include: country-specific variable names; questionnaire adaptations; education-system codes; language codes; variables omitted because a module was not administered; country-specific response categories; and occasional questionnaire or data-layout anomalies. Simply appending fs.sav files from several countries will therefore not produce a reliable multi-country analysis file. 18 Constructing research-ready reading variables The raw MICS6 reading data are unusually difficult to use correctly across countries. AFLEARN’s reading-processing script addresses four problems: multiple reading passages and languages; passage length, which is needed to calculate the 90% accuracy threshold; country-specific variable layouts and questionnaire adaptations; and complex skip patterns, which mean that a missing passage result can have several substantively different explanations. The goal is to turn the raw reading fields into variables that researchers can interpret without reconstructing the questionnaire routing every time. 18.1 The script The current AFLEARN script is harmonize-mics-reading-v1.1.R. It reads Data/UNICEF/ and writes to Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/. With the clean UNICEF folders in place, run: source("Script/harmonize-mics-reading-v1.1.R") The existing implementation writes: Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta with one child-level record per fs observation in the supported surveys and identifiers that allow the reading variables to be merged with the harmonised fs data or, later, an IPUMS MICS extract. 18.2 Why AFLEARN constructs additional reading variables 18.2.1 Problem 1: a country can have more than one passage In multilingual surveys, the original UNICEF file can contain more than one reading passage. The most important example for understanding the issue is Malawi, where children could be assessed in English and Chichewa. A research-ready dataset therefore needs to know: Which passage did this child attempt? │ ▼ What language was that passage? │ ▼ How long was that passage? This is also the reason the IPUMS reading variables should not be used in multi-passage MICS6 countries: as explained in Getting data from IPUMS MICS, IPUMS retains only one passage in these cases. 18.2.2 Problem 2: passage length is required for reading accuracy MICS foundational reading requires at least 90% of the passage words to be read correctly. If: words attempted = A words read incorrectly = I then: words read correctly = A - I But that is not enough to determine accuracy. We also need: L = total number of words in the passage so that: \[ \text{reading accuracy} = \frac{\text{words read correctly}} {\text{passage length}} \] The released country datasets do not provide one simple harmonised variable giving the length of the passage administered to each child. AFLEARN therefore constructs passage_language and passage_length. 18.2.3 Problem 3: missing reading results have different meanings Consider these children: Child A age 6 Child B age 10, caregiver did not consent Child C age 10, no suitable assessment language Child D age 10, child declined the story Child E age 10, failed the practice sequence Child F age 10, attempted the main passage A simple reading-score variable may be missing for A–E. But these children did not reach the same point in the assessment and should not automatically be treated as a single “missing reading data” category. AFLEARN therefore creates reading_status. 18.3 The reading_status variable The current harmonisation distinguishes: Code Reading assessment status 0 Not interviewed 1 Outside the FLS reading age range 2 Caregiver consent not given 3 Child consent not given 4 Assessment language mismatch 5 Child did not want to read the story 6 Failed the practice sentence/questions 7 Attempted a reading passage 8 Met the foundational-reading criterion 9 Not classified because the data are inconsistent with the expected routing This variable is useful for two different purposes. First, it makes sample construction transparent. Researchers can see why an age-eligible child has no passage score. Second, it makes data-quality checks easier. Code 9 deliberately identifies observations that cannot be reconciled cleanly with the expected questionnaire pathway rather than silently forcing them into another category. Do not recode all non-attempts as children who cannot read A child who was not assessed because an appropriate language was unavailable has not demonstrated the same thing as a child who attempted the passage and read no words correctly. 18.4 Reading outcomes in the harmonised file The current output includes variables such as: Variable Meaning passage_language Language of the main/primary passage passage_length Number of words in that passage words_att Words attempted words_incorrect Words missed/read incorrectly reading_score Words read correctly reading_accuracy Share of passage words read correctly read_comp_1–read_comp_5 Five comprehension items read_comp_score Number of comprehension items correct reading_skills Foundational-reading classification reading_status Assessment pathway/outcome *B* variables Corresponding fields for a second passage where applicable max_reading_* Best result across passages where more than one was attempted The output also retains: country_iso3 year HH1 HH2 LN cluster hhno linech so that it can be merged to both AFLEARN’s harmonised fs file and an IPUMS child extract. 18.5 Children who attempted more than one passage Some children attempted more than one reading passage. This is analytically different from a child who attempted only one. The AFLEARN processing retains passage-specific information and creates max_reading_* variables so that researchers can identify the best observed result across passages where this is appropriate for the research question. Researchers should state explicitly how multiple attempts are handled rather than silently choosing one. 18.6 Checking the output In R: library(haven) library(dplyr) reading <- read_dta( "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta" ) reading %>% count(country_iso3, year) reading %>% count(country_iso3, reading_status) summary(reading$reading_accuracy) Reading accuracy should normally fall between 0 and 1. Values outside that range should trigger investigation. You should also inspect the distribution of passage languages: reading %>% count(country_iso3, passage_language) and, for multi-passage countries, passage-specific attempt counts. 18.7 Merge reading onto the harmonised fs file In R: library(dplyr) fs <- haven::read_dta( "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_fs_harmonized.dta" ) reading <- haven::read_dta( "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta" ) analysis <- fs %>% left_join( reading, by = c( "country_iso3", "year", "HH1", "HH2", "LN" ), relationship = "one-to-one", suffix = c("", "_reading") ) Before merging, check that the keys are unique in both files. fs %>% count(country_iso3, year, HH1, HH2, LN) %>% filter(n > 1) reading %>% count(country_iso3, year, HH1, HH2, LN) %>% filter(n > 1) In Stata: use "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_fs_harmonized.dta", clear isid country_iso3 year HH1 HH2 LN merge 1:1 country_iso3 year HH1 HH2 LN using /// "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta" tab _merge 18.8 Implementing the 90% accuracy threshold AFLEARN implements the reading-accuracy threshold using the passage-specific word count and reproduces the classification used in MICS publications. Where 90% of the passage length is not an integer, AFLEARN uses the integer cutoff that reproduces the published MICS classification. This choice was validated empirically by comparing alternative classifications against published MICS results. The detailed validation and construction rules are documented in Reading-variable construction. 18.9 Next If you are using the original UNICEF data, you now have the core pieces required for analysis: harmonised fs data + research-ready reading data │ ▼ child-level analysis file Before estimating means, proportions, regressions or confidence intervals, read Survey design, weights and standard errors. If you instead want to combine these reading outcomes with an IPUMS MICS extract, see Adding the correct reading data to an IPUMS extract.

19 Adding the correct reading data to an IPUMS extract This page shows how to combine an IPUMS MICS child extract with AFLEARN’s research-ready MICS6 reading data. The purpose is to retain the main advantage of IPUMS — harmonised multi-country background variables — without using incomplete reading data in countries that administered multiple passages. In a multi-passage survey, children assessed in the passage IPUMS does not retain are absent from the harmonised reading variables. Because that absence is generated by the language in which a child was assessed, dropping observations with missing IPUMS reading variables does not solve the problem — it creates a systematically selected analysis sample. The limitation is set out in Getting data from IPUMS MICS. 19.1 AFLEARN’s solution AFLEARN constructs the reading variables from the original UNICEF MICS6 country files and retains all relevant passages. The reading file includes variables such as: passage_language passage_length words_att words_incorrect reading_score reading_accuracy read_comp_1 ... read_comp_5 read_comp_score reading_skills reading_status and passage-specific / multiple-attempt information where relevant. See Constructing research-ready reading variables for definitions. 19.2 The linking identifiers AFLEARN’s reading file deliberately retains both the original UNICEF identifiers and IPUMS-style linking identifiers. For linking to IPUMS, the relevant fields are: AFLEARN IPUMS -------------------------------- cluster <-> CLUSTER hhno <-> HHNO linech <-> LINECH survey/sample <-> SAMPLE IPUMS’s official linking guidance confirms that SAMPLE, CLUSTER, HHNO and the person line number are the key identifying variables in pooled extracts. The original MICS6 identifiers underlying these are: HH1 -> CLUSTER HH2 -> HHNO selected child's line number -> LINECH 19.3 Step 1: create your IPUMS child extract Choose: Unit of analysis: Children age 5–17 Select the MICS6 samples and background variables needed for your research. Make sure the resulting extract retains: SAMPLE CLUSTER HHNO LINECH or their corresponding automatically included technical identifiers. Run the IPUMS-provided Stata syntax to create the harmonised .dta file. See the IPUMS MICS extract instructions. 19.4 Step 2: obtain the AFLEARN reading file Use the AFLEARN-provided research-ready reading file, or construct it from the original UNICEF data using: harmonize-mics-reading-v1.1.R as described in Constructing research-ready reading variables. 19.5 Step 3: make the sample identifier compatible CLUSTER, HHNO and LINECH identify a child within a survey, but they are not sufficient for a pooled multi-country file because the same numbers occur in different surveys. You must therefore include the survey/sample identifier in the merge. AFLEARN’s reading file contains country and year identifiers from which the corresponding IPUMS sample can be mapped. We recommend creating an explicit crosswalk: AFLEARN country + year IPUMS SAMPLE ---------------------------------------- Malawi 2019/20 [sample code] Benin 2021 [sample code] ... and storing that crosswalk with the project. Do not guess IPUMS sample codes from country names Use the actual SAMPLE or SAMPLE_STR values in your extract and validate the mapping once. IPUMS sample identifiers distinguish survey year and, where necessary, national and subnational samples. 19.6 Step 4: check uniqueness before merging 19.6.1 R library(haven) library(dplyr) ipums <- read_dta("Data/IPUMS/ipums_mics_fs.dta") reading <- read_dta("Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta") ipums %>% count(SAMPLE, CLUSTER, HHNO, LINECH) %>% filter(n > 1) The AFLEARN file should be checked using the corresponding mapped sample identifier: reading %>% count(SAMPLE, cluster, hhno, linech) %>% filter(n > 1) If either check returns observations, investigate before merging. 19.6.2 Stata use "Data/IPUMS/ipums_mics_fs.dta", clear duplicates report SAMPLE CLUSTER HHNO LINECH and perform the corresponding check on the AFLEARN file after adding the IPUMS sample identifier. 19.7 Step 5: merge in R Assuming the AFLEARN file has been given the matching SAMPLE value: library(haven) library(dplyr) ipums <- read_dta("Data/IPUMS/ipums_mics_fs.dta") reading <- read_dta( "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta" ) analysis <- ipums %>% left_join( reading, by = c( "SAMPLE", "CLUSTER" = "cluster", "HHNO" = "hhno", "LINECH" = "linech" ), relationship = "one-to-one" ) The left_join() keeps the IPUMS child extract as the analysis population and adds AFLEARN reading information where available. 19.8 Step 6: merge in Stata Rename the AFLEARN identifiers to match IPUMS: use "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta", clear rename cluster CLUSTER rename hhno HHNO rename linech LINECH * SAMPLE must already have been mapped to the * corresponding IPUMS sample identifier. isid SAMPLE CLUSTER HHNO LINECH tempfile reading save `reading' use "Data/IPUMS/ipums_mics_fs.dta", clear merge 1:1 SAMPLE CLUSTER HHNO LINECH using `reading' tab _merge IPUMS’s own guidance uses the same underlying approach for linking additional variables from original UNICEF MICS files to an IPUMS extract. See IPUMS MICS Linking. 19.9 Step 7: inspect the merge Do not immediately drop unmatched records. In Stata: tab _merge SAMPLE In R, create an explicit match flag: analysis <- ipums %>% left_join( reading %>% mutate(aflearn_reading_match = TRUE), by = c( "SAMPLE", "CLUSTER" = "cluster", "HHNO" = "hhno", "LINECH" = "linech" ), relationship = "one-to-one" ) analysis %>% count(SAMPLE, aflearn_reading_match) Remember that not every fs child is expected to have a completed reading assessment. Children aged 5–6 and 15–17 are outside the FLS target age range, and eligible children can also follow other reading-status pathways. The important question is whether the child record links correctly, not whether every child has a non-missing reading score. 19.10 Step 8: remove or clearly distinguish the IPUMS reading variables For multi-passage surveys, we recommend removing the incomplete IPUMS reading outcome variables from the final analysis dataset once the AFLEARN variables have been added. This prevents accidental use later. For example, in R: analysis <- analysis %>% select( -FLWORDSATTEMPT # add other IPUMS reading variables to remove here ) or rename them clearly if you need to retain them for validation. In Stata: drop FLWORDSATTEMPT The final production script should list the complete set of IPUMS reading variables that should be excluded or replaced. Recommended principle In multi-passage countries, there should be only one clearly identified set of reading outcomes in the analysis file: the AFLEARN variables constructed from the complete UNICEF source data. 19.11 Step 9: validate the combined file At minimum, check: 19.11.1 Number of children by survey analysis %>% count(SAMPLE) 19.11.2 Reading status among children aged 7–14 analysis %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% count(SAMPLE, reading_status) Use the actual IPUMS age variable selected in your extract. 19.11.3 Passage language analysis %>% count(SAMPLE, passage_language) For a known multi-passage country such as Malawi, this is an important validation: both relevant assessment languages should be represented in the AFLEARN reading data. 19.11.4 Compare against the original UNICEF processing For supported surveys, aggregate results from the merged IPUMS + AFLEARN file should reproduce the corresponding results from the AFLEARN/UNICEF child-level analysis file, allowing for any intentional differences in the analysis sample. 19.12 A useful validation exercise for Malawi The Malawi case is a particularly clear test of whether the merge has worked. Before replacement, the IPUMS reading data identify only the retained English-passage observations in FLWORDSATTEMPT. After adding the AFLEARN reading file, the analysis should recover the Chichewa assessments as well. A simple validation table should show, by passage language: Malawi ----------------------------- English ... Chichewa ... Both ... and should reconcile with the original UNICEF source data. 19.13 What if I use only single-passage countries? If your analysis is restricted entirely to surveys with one reading passage, the specific multi-passage omission described here does not arise. However, AFLEARN’s reading variables still offer advantages: a consistent reading-status variable; harmonised passage metadata; consistent accuracy construction; and the same reading definitions across all supported MICS6 surveys. Using the AFLEARN reading file for all countries can therefore simplify a project and avoid maintaining different reading workflows for different surveys. 19.14 Next Once the IPUMS and AFLEARN data are combined, the next major issue is statistical rather than data management. Continue to Survey design, weights and standard errors before calculating population estimates, confidence intervals or regression standard errors.

20 Survey design, weights and standard errors MICS is a complex sample survey. To produce correct population estimates and standard errors, an analysis needs to account for the survey design. For the MICS6 selected-child (fs) data, three pieces of information are central: fsweight sampling weight for the selected child PSU primary sampling unit stratum sampling stratum The standard MICS6 files include these variables in the fs dataset. IPUMS also harmonises the corresponding survey-design variables. See the IPUMS MICS variable-name crosswalk. The basic rule For analysis of children in the fs file, do not calculate a weighted mean and then use an ordinary standard error. Tell the software about the weight, clustering and stratification together. This section explains: what the selected-child weight represents; why clustering and stratification matter; how to set up a MICS6 survey design in R and Stata; how to estimate subpopulations correctly; and what changes when several countries/surveys are combined. 20.1 Why ordinary standard errors are wrong MICS does not draw children independently from a simple random sample. Households are selected through a stratified, clustered sample design. Children living in the same sampled cluster can be more similar to one another than children selected independently from across the country. If the analysis ignores that structure, the estimated standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values can be wrong. Weights solve a different problem. They account for unequal selection probabilities and survey adjustments. They do not, by themselves, tell the software how observations are clustered or stratified. A correct design-based analysis therefore needs: WEIGHT + PSU / CLUSTER + STRATUM 20.2 The three design variables 20.2.1 fsweight fsweight is the sample weight for the randomly selected child aged 5–17. Use it when the unit of analysis is the selected child — including analyses of foundational reading and numeracy among children aged 7–14. 20.2.2 PSU PSU identifies the primary sampling unit used for sampling-error estimation. In most MICS applications this corresponds to the sampled cluster/enumeration area. Do not assume that the household identifier is the PSU. 20.2.3 stratum stratum identifies the sampling stratum used for variance estimation. Stratification is part of the sample design and should be incorporated when estimating standard errors. The exact design variables should always be checked in the country dataset and survey documentation. Some surveys contain additional working design variables, but standard MICS6 releases generally provide PSU and stratum. 20.3 Next The next page explains the two MICS6 weights found in the fs file and why fsweight is normally the correct choice for foundational-learning analysis: Which MICS weight should I use?.
