21 Which MICS weight should I use? MICS provides different weights for different questionnaire populations. For example, standard MICS6 files include weights such as: File/population Standard weight Household hhweight Women wmweight Men, where applicable mnweight Children under five chweight Selected children aged 5–17 fsweight The MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis explains that questionnaire-specific weights are attached to the corresponding datasets. 21.1 For foundational-learning analysis, normally use fsweight The FLS assessment is administered within the Questionnaire for Children Age 5–17, for which one eligible child is randomly selected per household. That extra within-household selection step matters. A child in a household containing several eligible 5–17-year-olds has a lower probability of being selected for fs than an otherwise comparable child who is the only eligible child in their household. fsweight accounts for the selected-child sampling process. So, for example: Outcome: foundational numeracy Population: children aged 7–14 in fs Weight: fsweight and: Outcome: reading accuracy Population: children who reached the reading passage Base analysis file: fs Weight: fsweight The fact that the outcome is defined only for a subgroup does not mean a new questionnaire weight is required. 21.2 The weight follows the analysis population, not the source of each variable Suppose you start with fs and merge household wealth from hh: fs: child learning outcome child age fsweight + hh: household wealth ↓ one row per selected child Your unit of analysis is still the selected child. Use: fsweight not: hhweight Similarly, adding a parent’s education from hl or another linked file does not turn the analysis into a household-member analysis. Ask “what does one row represent?” That question is usually more useful than asking which file a covariate originally came from. 21.3 What is fshweight? MICS6 fs files also commonly contain: fshweight labelled the Children 5–17 household sample weight. This is distinct from fsweight. For ordinary child-level analyses of the randomly selected 5–17-year-old — including FLS outcomes — use fsweight. The distinction is important because fsweight incorporates the selection of one child from the eligible 5–17-year-olds in the household, whereas the household-level weight does not represent each selected child with that within-household selection adjustment. 21.4 Do I need to divide the weight by 1,000 or another constant? Not for standard estimates of means, proportions or regression coefficients. Multiplying every weight in one survey by the same positive constant does not change a weighted mean or proportion. The MICS weights can therefore normally be supplied to survey software as released. Do not rescale weights simply because another survey programme uses a particular scaling convention. 21.5 A note on population totals MICS analysis weights are commonly normalised rather than expansion weights to a known national population total. That means they are appropriate for estimating proportions, means and relationships, but the sum of weights should not automatically be interpreted as the number of people in the national population. If your research question requires population counts or totals, consult the country sampling documentation and determine whether an additional population-calibration step is required. 21.6 Weighting does not replace the survey design This is not enough: weighted.mean(outcome, fsweight) and this is not enough for inference: mean outcome [pw=fsweight] These can produce a weighted point estimate, but they do not fully specify the clustered and stratified MICS design. For design-correct standard errors, set up the complete survey design as shown on the next page.

22 Setting up one MICS6 survey For a single MICS6 survey, the standard selected-child design uses: weight = fsweight PSU = PSU stratum = stratum This page shows how to set that design up in R and Stata. 22.1 First check the design variables Before creating a survey object: library(haven) library(dplyr) d <- read_dta("Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_fs_harmonized.dta") d %>% summarise( n = n(), missing_weight = sum(is.na(fsweight)), missing_psu = sum(is.na(PSU)), missing_stratum = sum(is.na(stratum)), n_psu = n_distinct(PSU), n_strata = n_distinct(stratum) ) If you are using the AFLEARN harmonised file, confirm the final exact capitalisation of PSU in the production version. You should also check how many PSUs occur within each stratum: d %>% distinct(stratum, PSU) %>% count(stratum, name = "n_psu") %>% arrange(n_psu) 22.2 R: the survey package library(survey) des <- svydesign( ids = ~PSU, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~fsweight, data = d, nest = TRUE ) nest = TRUE tells survey that PSU identifiers are nested within strata. This is a safe specification when PSU codes can repeat between strata. A weighted mean: svymean( ~pct_total_math, design = des, na.rm = TRUE ) A proportion for a 0/1 indicator: svymean( ~foundational_numeracy, design = des, na.rm = TRUE ) 22.3 R: srvyr for tidyverse-style analysis If you prefer dplyr syntax, srvyr wraps the survey package. library(srvyr) des <- d %>% as_survey_design( ids = PSU, strata = stratum, weights = fsweight, nest = TRUE ) Then: des %>% summarise( mean_math = survey_mean( pct_total_math, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = c("se", "ci") ) ) or by a subgroup: des %>% group_by(sex) %>% summarise( mean_math = survey_mean( pct_total_math, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = c("se", "ci") ) ) 22.4 Stata svyset PSU [pw=fsweight], strata(stratum) Check the design: svydescribe Then estimate, for example: svy: mean pct_total_math For a 0/1 foundational-numeracy indicator: svy: mean foundational_numeracy The mean of a variable coded 0/1 is the estimated proportion equal to 1. 22.5 Why not use HH1 automatically as the PSU? MICS datasets contain both the original cluster identifier (HH1) and design variables such as PSU. For many surveys these may correspond closely, but the safest approach is to use the sampling-error design variables supplied with the released data. In the standard MICS6 naming convention: PSU primary sampling unit stratum sample stratum IPUMS also harmonises these as PSU and STRATUM. 22.6 Lonely PSUs Variance estimation within a stratum relies on having more than one sampled PSU in that stratum. Occasionally, after restricting to a domain or because of a particular survey design, software may encounter a stratum with only one contributing PSU. In R, the survey package provides several options for handling these “lonely PSUs”. Do not choose one mechanically. First determine whether the problem exists in the full survey design or only after defining a subpopulation. A useful default for analysis workflows where lonely domains occur is: options( survey.lonely.psu = "adjust", survey.adjust.domain.lonely = TRUE ) but the chosen treatment should be documented. In Stata, inspect singleton-unit messages and the survey design rather than silently ignoring them. 22.7 Do not filter the raw data before defining the survey design This is especially important when estimating a subgroup. Suppose you want results for children aged 7–14. Avoid: # Not recommended for domain inference d_7_14 <- d %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) des <- svydesign( ids = ~PSU, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~fsweight, data = d_7_14, nest = TRUE ) Instead, define the survey design using the full relevant sample and then restrict the design object: des <- svydesign( ids = ~PSU, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~fsweight, data = d, nest = TRUE ) des_7_14 <- subset( des, age >= 7 & age <= 14 ) With srvyr: des_7_14 <- des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) This preserves the information survey software needs for correct domain/subpopulation variance estimation. 22.8 Stata subpopulations The same principle applies in Stata. Rather than physically dropping everyone outside the domain and then estimating: svy, subpop(if age >= 7 & age <= 14): /// mean pct_total_math For a more complex domain, create a 0/1 indicator: gen age7_14 = inrange(age,7,14) svy, subpop(age7_14): mean pct_total_math subpop() tells Stata that the target is a subpopulation of the original survey sample. 22.9 Next If your analysis contains more than one MICS survey, additional steps are required. 23 Combining MICS6 surveys Multi-country MICS analysis introduces two separate questions: How should the survey design be represented technically? What population does a pooled estimate represent? These should not be confused. Making PSU identifiers unique across countries solves a variance-estimation problem. It does not, by itself, make a pooled weighted mean a meaningful regional estimate. 23.1 Problem 1: PSU and stratum numbers repeat across surveys Suppose two surveys both contain: PSU = 1 stratum = 1 They are obviously not the same sampling unit or stratum. If surveys are appended without changing these identifiers, survey software can incorrectly treat unrelated observations as belonging to the same design units. The solution is to create identifiers that are unique to each survey. 23.2 Create a survey identifier For AFLEARN’s UNICEF-based harmonised data, a survey identifier can be based on: country_iso3 + year For IPUMS data, use the IPUMS sample identifier such as SAMPLE. Then create survey-specific PSU and stratum variables. 23.3 R library(dplyr) d <- d %>% mutate( survey_id = interaction( country_iso3, year, drop = TRUE ), psu_pool = interaction( survey_id, PSU, drop = TRUE ), stratum_pool = interaction( survey_id, stratum, drop = TRUE ) ) Then: library(survey) des_pool <- svydesign( ids = ~psu_pool, strata = ~stratum_pool, weights = ~fsweight, data = d, nest = TRUE ) 23.4 Stata egen survey_id = group(country_iso3 year) egen psu_pool = group(survey_id PSU) egen stratum_pool = group(survey_id stratum) svyset psu_pool [pw=fsweight], strata(stratum_pool) This tells the software correctly that a PSU in Malawi is not the same PSU as one carrying the same numeric code in Ghana. Always make both PSU and stratum identifiers survey-specific in appended data Doing only the PSU is not enough if stratum codes also repeat across surveys. 23.5 Estimating each country separately If the objective is: What is the mean numeracy score in each country? then you are estimating country-specific statistics, not one pooled population parameter. One transparent approach is to retain the combined design and estimate by country/survey. 23.5.1 R with srvyr des_pool %>% group_by(country_iso3) %>% summarise( mean_math = survey_mean( pct_total_math, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = c("se", "ci") ) ) 23.5.2 Stata svy: mean pct_total_math, over(country_iso3) or run country-specific estimates while retaining the correct survey design. For cross-country figures and tables, this is often exactly what you want. 23.6 Problem 2: what does a pooled mean mean? Suppose instead you calculate: one mean across all 18 countries What population is that intended to describe? There are several possibilities: the combined population of children in the 18 countries; the “average country”, giving each country equal weight; the average child represented by the collection of normalised survey samples; or some externally defined regional population. These are different estimands and require different weighting choices. 23.7 MICS country weights do not automatically create a population-weighted regional estimate MICS sample weights are constructed for inference within each survey and are generally normalised within the survey. If you simply append countries and use the released fsweight values: pooled mean using fsweight the relative contribution of one country versus another is driven partly by survey sample sizes and each survey’s weight normalisation. It should not automatically be interpreted as the proportion of all children across those countries. For a true population-weighted regional estimate, you would need external population information appropriate to the target population and survey reference periods, and construct weights accordingly. 23.8 Equal-country averages are another option Sometimes the research question is: What does the average result across these countries look like if every country contributes equally? A simple way is: estimate the statistic separately within each country using the correct MICS design; combine the country estimates with equal country weights. That estimand is an average of country estimates, not an estimate for the pooled child population. It should be labelled accordingly. 23.9 Regression across countries The same conceptual issue applies to pooled regressions. Creating psu_pool and stratum_pool correctly handles the fact that design units belong to different surveys. But you still need to decide: what the observation weights imply about the relative contribution of countries; whether country fixed effects are needed; whether coefficients are intended to describe within-country or between-country variation; and whether the target is an average relationship across the included surveys or a population-level regional relationship. There is no single automatic “MICS pooled weight” that answers every multi-country research question. Separate design from estimand psu_pool and stratum_pool tell the software how the observations were sampled. Your treatment of country weights tells the analysis what pooled population or average you are trying to represent. 23.10 Repeated surveys from the same country If you include two MICS6 surveys from the same country, such as different years or samples, the identifiers must still be survey-specific, not merely country-specific. Use: country + year/sample rather than country alone when creating pooled PSU and stratum identifiers. 23.11 Recommended workflow for comparative AFLEARN analyses For most descriptive comparisons in this guide: retain the released fsweight; make PSU and stratum identifiers unique by survey; define the combined survey design; estimate statistics separately by country/survey; and plot or compare those country estimates. Only create a single pooled regional statistic when the estimand and the required between-country weighting have been explicitly defined.

24 Getting standard errors right A point estimate and its uncertainty answer different questions. For example: Estimated foundational numeracy = 23% tells us the estimated population proportion. A standard error tells us how precisely that proportion has been estimated under the sample design. MICS analyses should therefore use design-based standard errors that account for: the selected-child weight; clustering within PSUs; and stratification. 24.1 A quick comparison Consider these three approaches: 1. unweighted mean + ordinary SE 2. weighted mean + ordinary SE 3. survey-weighted mean + design-based SE For population inference from MICS, the third is generally the appropriate approach. The first ignores unequal selection probabilities. The second incorporates weights into the point estimate but still ignores the clustered and stratified design in the variance calculation. 24.2 Confidence intervals A 95% confidence interval combines the estimate and its standard error. In R with srvyr: des %>% summarise( numeracy = survey_mean( foundational_numeracy, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = c("se", "ci") ) ) In Stata: svy: mean foundational_numeracy Both return design-based uncertainty once the survey design has been specified correctly. 24.3 Subgroups can become imprecise quickly MICS surveys are designed to produce reliable estimates for specified populations and reporting domains. A dataset containing thousands of children nationally can have far fewer effective observations once you estimate, for example: Grade 2 × rural × poorest quintile × one country Do not judge precision only from the raw number of child records. Check: number of sampled PSUs contributing to the estimate; standard error; confidence interval; and, where useful, coefficient of variation or design effect. 24.4 Design effects The design effect compares the variance under the actual complex design with a reference variance under simple random sampling. Values above 1 indicate that the complex design produces a larger variance than the simple-random-sample reference. Clustering often increases variance because children within the same PSU are correlated. Stratification can improve precision. In R, many survey/srvyr estimators can return a design effect. For example: svymean( ~pct_total_math, design = des, na.rm = TRUE, deff = TRUE ) Design effects are useful diagnostics, but they are not a substitute for actually specifying the survey design. 24.5 Degrees of freedom For complex survey inference, precision depends strongly on the number of independent sampled PSUs, not simply the number of child observations. Survey software therefore uses design-based degrees of freedom when constructing tests and confidence intervals. This is another reason that a regression with several thousand child records may still have much less independent information than the raw N suggests. 24.6 Missing outcomes If an outcome is missing, survey estimators generally omit those observations for that particular estimate when na.rm = TRUE or the corresponding Stata command handles missing values. But with reading, why the outcome is missing matters substantively. Before estimating reading performance, use AFLEARN’s reading_status to understand whether children: were outside the target age; did not have consent; faced an assessment-language mismatch; did not proceed through the reading sequence; or attempted the passage. Do not treat all missing reading values as a generic statistical nuisance. 24.7 Domain analysis, again Suppose the target is: Mean numeracy among out-of-school children aged 10–14. The safest sequence is: full selected-child survey data │ ▼ define survey design │ ▼ define age/schooling subpopulation │ ▼ estimate mean + design-based SE rather than: drop everyone else from raw data │ ▼ pretend remaining observations were the original survey sample In R, subset/filter the survey design object. In Stata, use subpop(). 24.8 Regressions also need the survey design The issue does not disappear when you move from descriptive statistics to regression. In R: model <- svyglm( pct_total_math ~ age + sex + wealth_quintile, design = des ) summary(model) In Stata: svy: regress pct_total_math /// c.age i.sex i.wealth_quintile For binary outcomes, use an appropriate survey-aware model rather than an ordinary model with weights added informally. 24.9 A practical reporting standard For descriptive MICS estimates, we recommend reporting enough information for readers to understand precision: estimate 95% confidence interval unweighted analytic N For detailed technical work, also retain: standard error number of PSUs number of strata design effect / CV where useful The unweighted N is useful context but should never be used as a substitute for the design-based uncertainty estimate.

25 Survey-design checklist Before reporting a MICS6 estimate, check the following. 25.1 Analysis population I know what one row in my analysis dataset represents. For FLS analysis, my observations are selected children from fs. If I merged variables from hh or hl, I have not changed the weight merely because the covariate came from another file. 25.2 Weight I am using fsweight for selected-child/FLS analysis. I am not using fshweight as a substitute for the selected-child weight. I understand that normalised survey weights are not automatically population-expansion weights for estimating national counts. 25.3 Survey design I have specified the PSU. I have specified the sampling stratum. I have specified the weight. My standard errors come from survey-aware estimation. For standard MICS6 fs data, this will usually be: weight = fsweight PSU = PSU stratum = stratum 25.4 Subpopulations I defined the survey design before restricting to my analytical subpopulation. In R, I subset/filter the survey design object. In Stata, I use subpop() where appropriate. I checked whether small domains leave too few PSUs for precise estimation. 25.5 Multiple surveys If I appended countries or survey years: I created a survey identifier. PSU identifiers are unique across surveys. stratum identifiers are unique across surveys. I have not interpreted a simple pooled fsweight estimate as a population-weighted regional statistic without defining the estimand. If I report an average across countries, I state how countries were weighted. 25.6 Reading I checked reading_status before defining my reading analysis sample. For multi-passage countries, I use the AFLEARN reading data rather than incomplete IPUMS reading variables. 25.7 Reporting I report confidence intervals or standard errors with the point estimates. I retain the unweighted analytic N. For very small subgroups, I check the number of contributing PSUs and the width of the confidence interval. If these boxes are checked, the analysis is much less likely to produce a precise-looking but incorrectly estimated MICS result. The worked examples in Section 6 apply these principles in R and Stata.

27 Prepare the analysis data All of the worked examples start from one child-level analysis file. For the UNICEF-based workflow, combine: mics6_fs_harmonized + mics6_reading_harmonized + survey design variables + household wealth (for the wealth example) 27.1 1. Read the harmonised files 27.1.1 R library(tidyverse) library(haven) library(survey) library(srvyr) fs <- read_dta( "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_fs_harmonized.dta" ) reading <- read_dta( "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta" ) Merge the reading variables: d <- fs %>% left_join( reading, by = c( "country_iso3", "year", "HH1", "HH2", "LN" ), relationship = "one-to-one", suffix = c("", "_reading") ) 27.1.2 Stata use "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_fs_harmonized.dta", clear merge 1:1 country_iso3 year HH1 HH2 LN using /// "Data/AFLEARN Harmonised Data/mics6_reading_harmonized.dta" tab _merge drop _merge 27.2 2. Retain PSU and stratum in the AFLEARN FS harmonisation The current AFLEARN harmonize-mics-fs-v1.0.R script retains fsweight but does not yet retain PSU and stratum. These variables should be added to the harmonised FS output before publishing the worked examples. They are standard MICS survey-design variables: PSU primary sampling unit stratum sampling stratum fsweight selected-child sampling weight After that small change, every worked example can use the same design specification. Do not replace this step by clustering on HH1 without checking Use the sampling-error variables supplied in the MICS data. 27.3 3. Create identifiers that are unique across surveys Because PSU and stratum codes can repeat across countries and years, create pooled identifiers. 27.3.1 R d <- d %>% mutate( survey_id = paste(country_iso3, year, sep = "_"), psu_pool = interaction( survey_id, PSU, drop = TRUE ), stratum_pool = interaction( survey_id, stratum, drop = TRUE ) ) 27.3.2 Stata egen survey_id = group(country_iso3 year) egen psu_pool = group(survey_id PSU) egen stratum_pool = group(survey_id stratum) 27.4 4. Create the survey design 27.4.1 R des <- d %>% as_survey_design( ids = psu_pool, strata = stratum_pool, weights = fsweight, nest = TRUE ) 27.4.2 Stata svyset psu_pool [pw=fsweight], strata(stratum_pool) 27.5 5. Construct common numeracy measures The AFLEARN FS file currently retains the harmonised item responses but does not derive numeracy scores. The standard harmonised names are: number_id_* 6 number-identification items number_compare_* 5 number-discrimination items number_add_* 5 addition items number_pattern_* 5 number-pattern items Responses are coded so that: 1 = correct 2 = incorrect 3 = no attempt The standard questionnaire also contains stop rules. For a descriptive total-correct score, this guide scores an administered item as 1 if correct and 0 otherwise, and scores items not reached because of the numeracy stop rule as 0 for children who participated in the FLS assessment. This produces a score from 0 to 21. 27.5.1 R helper score_correct <- function(x) { case_when( x == 1 ~ 1, x %in% c(2, 3) ~ 0, TRUE ~ NA_real_ ) } num_items <- c( grep("^number_id_", names(d), value = TRUE), grep("^number_compare_", names(d), value = TRUE), grep("^number_add_", names(d), value = TRUE), grep("^number_pattern_", names(d), value = TRUE) ) length(num_items) # should be 21 Create item scores: d <- d %>% mutate( across( all_of(num_items), score_correct, .names = "{.col}_score" ) ) For children with a completed/usable FLS assessment, derive: score_vars <- paste0(num_items, "_score") d <- d %>% rowwise() %>% mutate( numeracy_total = if_else( age >= 7 & age <= 14 & fl_child_result == 1, sum(c_across(all_of(score_vars)), na.rm = TRUE), NA_real_ ) ) %>% ungroup() Before publication, AFLEARN should validate this total-score construction against the questionnaire routing in each supported survey. 27.6 6. Construct task-level measures For descriptive analysis, calculate the number correct in each domain: d <- d %>% rowwise() %>% mutate( n_number_id = sum( c_across(starts_with("number_id_") & ends_with("_score")), na.rm = TRUE ), n_number_compare = sum( c_across(starts_with("number_compare_") & ends_with("_score")), na.rm = TRUE ), n_number_add = sum( c_across(starts_with("number_add_") & ends_with("_score")), na.rm = TRUE ), n_number_pattern = sum( c_across(starts_with("number_pattern_") & ends_with("_score")), na.rm = TRUE ) ) %>% ungroup() The final production version should also include a validated foundational_numeracy variable reproducing the published MICS indicator. 27.7 7. Check everything before analysis At minimum: d %>% count(country_iso3, year) summary(d$fsweight) d %>% summarise( missing_psu = sum(is.na(PSU)), missing_stratum = sum(is.na(stratum)) ) table(d$reading_status, useNA = "ifany") summary(d$numeracy_total) The worked examples assume these checks have passed.

In standard MICS coding: 1 = yes 2 = no 28.4.1 R des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% mutate( in_school = enrolled == 1 ) %>% group_by(country_iso3, age) %>% summarise( enrolled_share = survey_mean( in_school, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 28.4.2 Stata gen in_school = enrolled == 1 if enrolled < . svy, subpop(if inrange(age,7,14)): /// mean in_school, over(country_iso3 age) 28.5 A useful first figure Plot school attendance by age for each country. Suggested design: x-axis: age 7–14 y-axis: proportion currently attending line: country This immediately shows how much the composition of the assessed population differs across countries as children get older. 28.6 Interpretation The important point is not simply whether school attendance is high or low. MICS allows researchers to see that: the learning assessment population is defined by age and household sampling, not school enrolment; out-of-school children remain part of the target population; and the composition of children in a particular grade can differ substantially across countries. This is one reason age-based and grade-based learning estimates answer different questions. 28.7 Output to add after running Add: a figure of current attendance by age; a small table showing the unweighted fs N and FLS-age N by survey; and one paragraph noting the main cross-country patterns.

29 Worked example 2: Indicators versus distributions 29.1 Research question Does the headline foundational-numeracy indicator tell the same story as the underlying distribution of numeracy performance? MICS6 contains 21 numeracy items across four domains: 6 number-identification items; 5 number-discrimination items; 5 addition items; and 5 number-pattern items. A binary indicator is useful for communication, but it compresses a large amount of information. 29.2 Construct the total score Using the preparation code, define: numeracy_total = number of items correct out of 21 The production version should also contain: foundational_numeracy validated against published MICS tabulations. 29.3 Compare the two measures 29.3.1 R num_des <- des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) num_des %>% group_by(country_iso3) %>% summarise( mean_score = survey_mean( numeracy_total, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ), foundational = survey_mean( foundational_numeracy, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 29.3.2 Stata svy, subpop(if inrange(age,7,14)): /// mean numeracy_total foundational_numeracy, /// over(country_iso3) 29.4 Look at the score distribution For one country: des %>% filter( country_iso3 == "MWI", age >= 7, age <= 14 ) %>% group_by(numeracy_total) %>% summarise( share = survey_mean( proportion = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE ) ) A histogram or weighted frequency plot can make the distribution visible. 29.5 Compare the four domains des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% group_by(country_iso3) %>% summarise( number_id = survey_mean( n_number_id / 6, na.rm = TRUE ), compare = survey_mean( n_number_compare / 5, na.rm = TRUE ), addition = survey_mean( n_number_add / 5, na.rm = TRUE ), pattern = survey_mean( n_number_pattern / 5, na.rm = TRUE ) ) These are average shares of items correct, not the official MICS task indicators. Label them accordingly. 29.6 Why this matters Consider two children: Child A: 20/21 Child B: 4/21 A stringent binary proficiency measure can classify both below the benchmark even though their observed skill profiles are very different. This matters particularly when: overall proficiency is low; comparing socioeconomic groups; studying progress by grade; or diagnosing which components of numeracy are most difficult. 29.7 Suggested figure A useful two-panel publication figure would show: Panel A: % meeting foundational numeracy Panel B: mean total score out of 21 for the same countries. The comparison makes visible where the ranking or apparent size of cross-country differences changes when the full score distribution is used. 29.8 Output to add after running Add: country means and confidence intervals; the proficiency estimates; one example score distribution; and a brief discussion of where the binary indicator compresses meaningful variation.

30 Worked example 3: Why is the reading outcome missing? 30.1 Research question When a child has no reading score, what happened in the assessment? A missing reading score does not have one meaning. AFLEARN’s reading_status reconstructs the reading pathway. The current coding is: Code Meaning 0 Not interviewed 1 Outside FLS reading age 2 Caregiver consent not given 3 Child consent not given 4 Assessment-language mismatch 5 Child did not want to read the story 6 Failed the practice sentence/questions 7 Attempted a reading passage 8 Met the foundational-reading criterion 9 Not classified / inconsistent routing Codes 7 and 8 both indicate that the child reached the passage; code 8 additionally identifies children meeting the foundational-reading criterion. 30.2 Describe the pathway among ages 7–14 30.2.1 R reading_status_tab <- des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% group_by(country_iso3, reading_status) %>% summarise( share = survey_mean( proportion = TRUE, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 30.2.2 Stata svy, subpop(if inrange(age,7,14)): /// proportion reading_status, over(country_iso3) 30.3 A simpler attempted/not-attempted distinction d <- d %>% mutate( reading_attempted = reading_status %in% c(7, 8) ) Then: des <- d %>% as_survey_design( ids = psu_pool, strata = stratum_pool, weights = fsweight, nest = TRUE ) des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% group_by(country_iso3) %>% summarise( attempted = survey_mean( reading_attempted, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 30.4 Why not code all non-attempts as zero reading skill? Because these categories describe different processes. For example: language mismatch means the survey could not offer an appropriate reading passage under the questionnaire routing. That is not direct evidence that the child cannot read. Similarly, lack of caregiver consent is a nonresponse event, not an observed low score. By contrast, failing the practice sequence is much closer to evidence about the child’s reading performance. The appropriate treatment depends on the research question. 30.5 Recommended reporting Whenever reading results exclude a substantial share of age-eligible children, report: % of target-age children with an attempted passage alongside the learning outcome. This makes assessment coverage visible rather than allowing it to disappear into missing values. 30.6 Suggested figure A stacked bar by country: attempted passage practice-route non-attempt language mismatch consent/refusal other Keep categories substantively meaningful rather than displaying all ten numeric codes if several are rare. 30.7 Output to add after running Add one figure and identify countries where assessment coverage is materially lower than the nominal 7–14 target population.

32 Worked example 5: Learning inequalities by wealth 32.1 Research question Do wealth inequalities look the same when learning is measured using a binary proficiency indicator versus the full score distribution? This example illustrates why outcome choice matters. When overall proficiency is very low, children in both the poorest and richest quintiles may mostly fall below the benchmark. A binary indicator can therefore make the groups look more similar than their underlying performance actually is. 32.2 Data requirement The current AFLEARN FS harmonised file does not contain wealth. Add: windex5 from the household file, or request WINDEX5 in an IPUMS extract. Standard MICS wealth quintiles are: 1 poorest 2 second 3 middle 4 fourth 5 richest 32.3 Compare proficiency by wealth 32.3.1 R des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% group_by(country_iso3, windex5) %>% summarise( foundational_num = survey_mean( foundational_numeracy, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 32.3.2 Stata svy, subpop(if inrange(age,7,14)): /// mean foundational_numeracy, /// over(country_iso3 windex5) 32.4 Compare average numeracy score by wealth 32.4.1 R des %>% filter(age >= 7, age <= 14) %>% group_by(country_iso3, windex5) %>% summarise( mean_num = survey_mean( numeracy_total, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 32.4.2 Stata svy, subpop(if inrange(age,7,14)): /// mean numeracy_total, /// over(country_iso3 windex5) 32.5 Focus on poorest versus richest A compact inequality measure is the richest-poorest difference. In R, first estimate each quintile and then calculate the contrast, or use a survey regression. model <- svyglm( numeracy_total ~ factor(windex5), design = subset( des, age >= 7 & age <= 14 ) ) summary(model) The coefficient on the richest category relative to the poorest gives the adjusted-by-design difference in mean score, with no other covariates. 32.6 Why the two inequality measures can differ Imagine: Poorest: mean 5/21, proficiency 1% Richest: mean 10/21, proficiency 4% The proficiency gap is only three percentage points, but the average score differs by five items. The benchmark is not wrong. It answers a different question: What share reaches a demanding threshold? The mean score asks: How far through the observed skill progression are children? For inequality analysis, showing both is often more informative. 32.7 Suggested figure For each country, plot two wealth gradients: Panel A: proficiency by wealth quintile Panel B: mean score by wealth quintile Use the same quintile ordering and clearly different y-axis labels. 32.8 Extension to reading The same logic can be applied to: max_reading_skills max_reading_accuracy max_reading_score provided the reading analysis sample and reading_status are handled explicitly. 32.9 Output to add after running Select two or three countries that illustrate different patterns rather than reproducing all countries in the body of the guide. The full results can remain in downloadable code/output.

33 Worked example 6: In-school and out-of-school children 33.1 Research question 33.2 Define current schooling status 33.3 Why compare within age? 33.4 Descriptive comparison by age 33.5 Age-adjusted comparison 33.6 Reading 33.7 Interpretation 33.8 Suggested figure

33 Worked example 6: In-school and out-of-school children 33.1 Research question At the same age, how does learning differ between children who are currently in school and those who are out of school? This is one of the distinctive advantages of a household-based learning assessment. A school-based assessment cannot observe children who are not enrolled or not attending the sampled schools. MICS can. 33.2 Define current schooling status The harmonised variable: enrolled records whether the child attended school or an early childhood education programme during the current school year. For school-age analysis: d <- d %>% mutate( in_school = case_when( enrolled == 1 ~ 1, enrolled == 2 ~ 0, TRUE ~ NA_real_ ) ) Re-create the design object after adding the variable. 33.3 Why compare within age? A simple comparison of all in-school and out-of-school children can be misleading because the groups may have very different age distributions. Older adolescents are more likely to have left school in many settings and have also had more potential exposure to schooling. Compare children of the same age, or adjust for age. 33.4 Descriptive comparison by age 33.4.1 R des %>% filter( age >= 10, age <= 14 ) %>% group_by( country_iso3, age, in_school ) %>% summarise( mean_num = survey_mean( numeracy_total, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 33.4.2 Stata svy, subpop(if inrange(age,10,14)): /// mean numeracy_total, /// over(country_iso3 age in_school) 33.5 Age-adjusted comparison 33.5.1 R model <- svyglm( numeracy_total ~ factor(age) + factor(in_school), design = subset( des, age >= 10 & age <= 14 ) ) summary(model) This estimates the association between current school attendance and numeracy conditional on age. It is not a causal estimate of the effect of attending school. Children who remain in school differ from children who leave school in many observed and unobserved ways. 33.6 Reading The same analysis can be performed for reading, but first define the relevant reading population using reading_status. For example: read_des <- des %>% filter( age >= 10, age <= 14, reading_status %in% c(7, 8) ) Then compare: max_reading_accuracy or another clearly defined reading outcome. 33.7 Interpretation The value of this analysis is descriptive: What learning levels are observed among children who are currently in school and among children who are not, at comparable ages? Do not write: School attendance increases numeracy by X points. The household-survey data do not identify that causal effect without a separate research design. 33.8 Suggested figure For ages 10–14: x-axis: age y-axis: mean numeracy score two lines: in school / out of school Facet by country or select illustrative countries. Also show the number of out-of-school observations contributing to each estimate; some age-country cells may be too small for useful inference.

34 Worked example 7: Learning by grade and age 34.1 Research question 34.2 First: construct a meaningful grade variable 34.3 Mean numeracy by primary grade 34.4 Now examine age within grade 34.5 Age and grade are jointly informative 34.6 Suggested figure 34.7 Cross-country trajectory tests

34 Worked example 7: Learning by grade and age 34.1 Research question How does learning change across grades, and how should we interpret differences when children of different ages occupy the same grade? Grade trajectories are intuitive, but MICS requires more care than a school-based grade assessment. 34.2 First: construct a meaningful grade variable The AFLEARN harmonised variable: current_grade is the year within the education level. It cannot be treated as a universal grade number without current_level_h. For primary school: d_primary <- d %>% filter( enrolled == 1, current_level_h == 1 ) Within this restricted group, current_grade can be interpreted as primary year/grade. If you want a single grade scale spanning primary and secondary, construct it from the country’s education system rather than simply using current_grade. See Why current_grade is not the child’s grade. 34.3 Mean numeracy by primary grade 34.3.1 R des %>% filter( age >= 7, age <= 14, enrolled == 1, current_level_h == 1, current_grade >= 1, current_grade <= 6 ) %>% group_by( country_iso3, current_grade ) %>% summarise( mean_num = survey_mean( numeracy_total, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) 34.3.2 Stata gen primary = current_level_h == 1 svy, subpop(if inrange(age,7,14) & enrolled==1 & /// primary & inrange(current_grade,1,6)): /// mean numeracy_total, /// over(country_iso3 current_grade) 34.4 Now examine age within grade 34.4.1 R des %>% filter( enrolled == 1, current_level_h == 1 ) %>% group_by( country_iso3, current_grade ) %>% summarise( mean_age = survey_mean( age, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE ) ) A country with an average age of 10.5 in Grade 3 is not compositionally identical to one with an average age of 8.5 in Grade 3. Late entry, repetition and interruptions to schooling all affect the relationship between age and grade. 34.5 Age and grade are jointly informative A useful model is: model <- svyglm( numeracy_total ~ factor(current_grade) + age, design = subset( des, enrolled == 1 & current_level_h == 1 & age >= 7 & age <= 14 ) ) summary(model) This describes grade differences after accounting linearly for age. Again, it is descriptive rather than causal. 34.6 Suggested figure For each country: x-axis: primary grade y-axis: mean numeracy score line: country and accompany it with a second figure/table showing mean age by grade. This prevents the trajectory graph from being interpreted as if every country’s Grade 3 population had the same age composition. 34.7 Cross-country trajectory tests If the research question is whether the shape of the grade trajectory differs across countries, use a regression with country-by-grade interactions rather than eyeballing the plot. For a flexible quadratic trajectory: model <- svyglm( numeracy_total ~ factor(country_iso3) * (current_grade + I(current_grade^2)), design = subset( des, enrolled == 1 & current_level_h == 1 & current_grade >= 1 & current_grade <= 6 ) ) Jointly test the country-by-grade interaction terms. In Stata: svy: regress numeracy_total /// i.country_iso3##c.current_grade##c.current_grade /// if enrolled==1 & current_level_h==1 & /// inrange(current_grade,1,6) testparm i.country_iso3#c.current_grade /// i.country_iso3#c.current_grade#c.current_grade The interaction test asks whether the trajectories differ across countries, not merely whether average performance levels differ.

35 Worked example 8: Timing within the school year 35.1 Research question If two children are both labelled “Grade 3”, have they necessarily had the same amount of exposure to Grade 3 instruction? No. MICS fieldwork can occur at different points in the school year across countries. A Grade 3 child assessed one month after the school year begins has had less Grade 3 exposure than a Grade 3 child assessed near the end of the year. This matters when interpreting cross-country grade trajectories. 35.2 What you need AFLEARN’s harmonised FS file already contains: interview_month but the current processing does not contain a harmonised variable measuring the child’s position within the country’s school year. For this example, create: school_month where: 0 = beginning of school year 1 = one month after beginning ... This requires a country-level lookup table giving the school-year start month. 35.3 Example lookup Illustrative structure: country_iso3 school_start_month BEN ... GHA ... MWI ... The values must be verified from country education calendars or survey documentation before publication. 35.4 Convert interview month to months through school year 35.4.1 R d <- d %>% left_join( school_calendar, by = "country_iso3" ) %>% mutate( school_month = ( interview_month - school_start_month ) %% 12 ) Depending on survey timing and holidays, a simple month difference may need country-specific adjustment. 35.5 Construct grade progress For children in a comparable grade system: d <- d %>% mutate( gradeprogress = current_grade + school_month / 12 ) Thus: Grade 3, start of year ≈ 3.0 Grade 3, six months in ≈ 3.5 Grade 4, start of year ≈ 4.0 This is an approximation to instructional exposure, not a literal measure of time in school. 35.6 Fit a trajectory 35.6.1 R model <- svyglm( numeracy_total ~ factor(country_iso3) * (gradeprogress + I(gradeprogress^2)), design = subset( des, enrolled == 1 & current_level_h == 1 & gradeprogress >= 1 & gradeprogress <= 6 ) ) summary(model) Test whether trajectories differ across countries: library(regTermTest) regTermTest( model, ~ factor(country_iso3):gradeprogress + factor(country_iso3):I(gradeprogress^2) ) Depending on the fitted model and package behaviour, the exact joint-test syntax may need adjustment. The production script should verify the coefficient names and test matrix explicitly. 35.6.2 Stata gen gradeprogress = current_grade + school_month/12 svy: regress numeracy_total /// i.country_iso3##c.gradeprogress##c.gradeprogress /// if enrolled==1 & current_level_h==1 & /// inrange(gradeprogress,1,6) testparm i.country_iso3#c.gradeprogress /// i.country_iso3#c.gradeprogress#c.gradeprogress 35.7 Predicted trajectories In Stata: margins country_iso3, /// at(gradeprogress=(1(0.25)6)) marginsplot In R, generate a prediction grid and use predict() with standard errors, or use a survey-compatible marginal-estimation package after verifying its handling of svyglm. 35.8 Why this example is more advanced gradeprogress solves only one comparability problem. It does not account for: differences in official school-entry age; grade repetition; interruptions to schooling; variation in instructional time; attendance; curriculum differences; or differences in the meaning of grade across education systems. It should therefore be described as an adjustment for survey timing within the school year, not a complete measure of schooling exposure. 35.9 Suggested use in the guide Keep this as the final, advanced worked example. It demonstrates how the rich timing information in MICS can improve cross-country comparisons while also showing why researchers need to be explicit about the assumptions behind derived variables.

37 FS harmonisation methods The FS harmonisation creates one child-level multi-country dataset from the original UNICEF MICS6 fs.sav files. The current script is: harmonize-mics-fs-v1.0.R 37.1 Pipeline For each supported survey, the script: identify survey from folder ↓ read fs.sav ↓ read hl.sav where required ↓ harmonise each thematic block ↓ apply country-specific mappings ↓ retain identifiers and merge keys ↓ append surveys ↓ apply labels ↓ write R, Stata and Excel outputs The current thematic blocks are: Theme Contents HH geography and household size WT selected-child weights INT FS interview date/time BG parent education and school type CB schooling background CL child labour PR parental involvement FCF child functioning FCD child discipline FL FLS setup and numeracy items Reading item batteries are intentionally excluded and handled by the separate reading script. 37.2 Identifiers Within each survey, the FS child is identified by: HH1 + HH2 + LN The script also creates: cluster = HH1 hhno = HH2 linech = LN to facilitate links to IPUMS and to the separate reading file. Before appending a survey, the processing should verify that: HH1 + HH2 + LN uniquely identifies each selected-child record. 37.3 Geography The harmonised fields include: Harmonised Standard source Meaning urban HH6 Urban/rural region HH7 First administrative region n_children_5_17 HH52 Children aged 5–17 in household region retains country-specific codes. A value of 1 in two countries does not imply the same type of region. Do not pool region codes without building a separate cross-country geographic classification. 37.4 Survey-design variables The current script retains: fsweight fshweight Before the revised guide is published, it should also retain: PSU stratum because these are needed for the survey-design workflow in Sections 5 and 6. No transformation is required: these should be preserved from the source data and documented in the crosswalk. 37.5 Interview timing The harmonised FS file retains: interview_day interview_month interview_year interview_start_hour interview_start_min interview_end_hour interview_end_min These are renamed from the standard FS interview fields. AFLEARN does not currently create a single derived interview date or interview duration. The interview_month variable is used in the advanced Section 6 example on timing within the school year. 37.6 Parent education Mother and father education illustrate why some harmonisation requires more than renaming. The raw country-specific variables are retained: mother_edu father_edu and common broad education levels are added: mother_edu_h father_edu_h The harmonised level codes are: Code Meaning 0 Early childhood / pre-primary 1 Primary 2 Lower secondary 3 Upper secondary 4 Vocational / technical 5 Higher / tertiary 8 Don’t know 9 No response / other special The country-specific mappings are stored in the processing script and written to the level_map sheet of the Excel crosswalk. 37.6.1 Father’s education Father education is not consistently available directly in fs.sav. The script uses the household-list file (hl.sav) and links the relevant household member onto the selected child’s row. This is a good example of why the output should be treated as a constructed research dataset rather than a simple renamed copy of fs.sav. 37.7 School type school_type is retained using the country source coding. It is not fully harmonised across countries. For example, some surveys use a standard public/religious/private/community classification, while others use a different institutional taxonomy. Use the country notes before pooling this variable. 37.8 Child schooling The main harmonised variables are: ever_attended highest_level highest_grade highest_completed enrolled current_level current_grade attended_previous previous_level previous_grade The raw level variables retain country coding. AFLEARN additionally constructs: highest_level_h current_level_h previous_level_h using the common broad education-level classification above. 37.8.1 Grade is deliberately not fully harmonised current_grade remains the year within the education level. For example: current_level_h = primary current_grade = 1 and: current_level_h = lower secondary current_grade = 1 both occur. These are different years in the education system. See Why current_grade is not the child’s grade. 37.9 Child labour, parental involvement, functioning and discipline For these themes the current harmonisation is intentionally conservative. It generally: renames common items retains original response coding applies common labels where justified does not manufacture derived indicators The script therefore does not automatically construct: child-labour prevalence; violent-discipline indicators; Washington Group functional-difficulty composites; or other higher-level policy indicators. Researchers who need those measures should derive them transparently from the harmonised items and the relevant indicator definitions. 37.10 Numeracy The FS harmonisation retains: number_id_* number_compare_* number_add_* number_pattern_* together with FLS setup variables such as: fl_consent child_consent lang_home lang_school fl_child_result It does not currently derive a foundational-numeracy indicator. Section 6 provides a provisional total-score workflow, but any official binary indicator should be validated against published MICS tabulations before being added to the harmonised product. 37.11 What the FS harmonisation deliberately does not do A common variable name should not imply more comparability than the source data support. The script therefore avoids: recoding region into a false cross-country taxonomy; treating raw school-type codes as universally identical; converting grade-within-level directly into years of schooling; deriving complex policy indicators without an explicit validation step; and duplicating reading variables already processed in the reading file.

38 Reading-variable construction 38.1 Pipeline 38.2 Reading score 38.3 Passage language 38.4 Passage length 38.5 Reading accuracy 38.6 Comprehension 38.7 Foundational-reading classification 38.8 Multiple passages 38.9 Malawi 38.10 Practice items 38.11 reading_status 38.12 Output variables

38 Reading-variable construction The reading harmonisation is the most technically involved part of the AFLEARN MICS6 workflow. The current script is: harmonize-mics-reading-v1.1.R Its purpose is to transform survey-specific reading variables into a consistent child-level file while retaining the information required to understand which language and passage each child was assessed in. 38.1 Pipeline For each survey: identify survey ↓ repair questionnaire-numbering differences ↓ rename reading variables ↓ repair known source-data problems ↓ identify passage language ↓ derive passage length ↓ handle second/third passages ↓ construct word + comprehension scores ↓ construct reading accuracy ↓ construct foundational-reading classification ↓ classify reading-status pathway ↓ retain merge identifiers 38.2 Reading score For a passage: reading_score = words attempted - words read incorrectly or: \[ \text{reading score} = \text{words attempted} - \text{words incorrect} \] The same structure is retained separately for additional passages where relevant. 38.3 Passage language For single-language surveys, the passage language can be assigned directly. For multilingual surveys, the language often needs to be inferred using survey-specific combinations of: language of instruction; home language; story selected; passage attempted; and country questionnaire routing. This is why passage_language is a constructed variable, not merely a renamed questionnaire field. 38.4 Passage length Reading accuracy requires the number of words in the passage. The current script derives passage length from the observed source data, generally using the maximum number of words attempted among children assigned to the relevant passage language: \[ L_l = \max(\text{words attempted}\mid\text{passage language}=l) \] where \(L_l\) is the inferred length of passage language \(l\). The resulting variable is: passage_length with equivalent fields for additional passages. 38.4.1 Validation requirement A data-derived passage length should always be checked. If no child reaches the end of a passage, the observed maximum can underestimate its true length. Validation should therefore include: maximum observed words attempted questionnaire/story text where available range of derived reading_accuracy published survey information A derived accuracy greater than 1 is an immediate warning that passage length or source counts require investigation. 38.5 Reading accuracy AFLEARN defines: \[ \text{reading accuracy} = \frac{\text{reading score}} {\text{passage length}} \] The output variable is: reading_accuracy with passage-specific equivalents where applicable. 38.6 Comprehension The standard reading assessment contains five comprehension questions. AFLEARN retains: read_comp_1 read_comp_2 read_comp_3 read_comp_4 read_comp_5 and constructs: read_comp_score as the number answered correctly, conditional on the relevant comprehension sequence having been administered. Country-specific source-variable mappings are handled before the score is constructed. 38.7 Foundational-reading classification The current AFLEARN construction combines: reading accuracy + comprehension The implementation uses the passage-specific integer word cutoff that reproduces the classifications in published MICS outputs. Where 90% of passage length is not an integer, AFLEARN uses a rounded-down word-count cutoff because validation against published MICS classifications showed that this reproduced the MICS results. The current implementation is conceptually: cutoff <- trunc(0.9 * passage_length) reading_skills = reading_score >= cutoff & comprehension criterion met This rounding convention is therefore intentional, not a numerical approximation introduced by the guide. Whenever the reading script is changed, the resulting classifications should again be checked against published country results. 38.8 Multiple passages A second or third passage is not treated as generic missingness. The script retains passage-specific variables where needed and builds summary fields such as: max_reading_score max_reading_accuracy max_reading_skills For children with more than one valid attempt, these represent the best observed result across relevant passages. Researchers should state explicitly when these max_* outcomes are used. 38.9 Malawi Malawi requires special treatment because English and Chichewa are stored as separate passages. Some children attempt only Chichewa. The script therefore moves Chichewa-only attempts into the primary analysis slots while retaining the passage-language information. This ensures that the combined reading file contains the complete assessment rather than treating the English passage as if it were the entire Malawi reading sample. 38.10 Practice items The reading pathway includes a practice sequence. AFLEARN retains the practice items and constructs: practice_outcome fail_practice These are important because children who fail the practice sequence may never reach the main passage. A missing main-passage score is therefore not sufficient to distinguish low performance from other assessment pathways. 38.11 reading_status AFLEARN constructs: Code Meaning 0 Not interviewed 1 Outside FLS reading age 2 Caregiver consent not given 3 Child consent not given 4 Assessment-language mismatch 5 Child did not want to read story 6 Failed practice 7 Attempted a reading passage 8 Met foundational-reading criterion 9 Not classified / inconsistent routing The order of assignment matters. Later observed outcomes overwrite earlier provisional categories where appropriate; code 9 catches observations that remain inconsistent with the expected routing. The purpose is not just convenience. reading_status makes the denominator and assessment pathway visible to analysts. 38.12 Output variables The research-ready reading file contains, where applicable: country_iso3 year HH1 HH2 LN cluster hhno linech reading_status passage_language passage_length words_att words_incorrect reading_score reading_accuracy read_comp_1 ... read_comp_5 read_comp_score practice_* practice_outcome reading_skills passage-B/C equivalents max_reading_* The technical script remains the authoritative record of the exact processing sequence.

39 Country-specific issues MICS6 is highly standardised, but country datasets are not identical. The AFLEARN harmonisation therefore contains explicit country-specific logic. This page summarises the issues already identified in the current processing system. The processing scripts and Excel crosswalk remain the authoritative implementation record. 39.1 Reading-specific issues Survey/country Issue AFLEARN treatment Sierra Leone Some records have attempted/incorrect word counts reversed Swap where attempted is below incorrect and the incorrect count is observed Zimbabwe Comprehension variables use a shifted numbering pattern Rename before common processing Comoros Some comprehension variables are offset within the FL21B* series Apply targeted renaming rather than shifting the entire block São Tomé and Príncipe Word counts can remain populated after early refusal/practice failure Clear counts before constructing reading scores Madagascar Similar early-refusal issue; multiple passage blocks also require cleaning Clear invalid passage-specific counts before scoring Central African Republic Early refusal/practice routing can leave word counts Clear invalid counts before scoring Malawi English and Chichewa stored as separate passages; some children attempt Chichewa only Retain both passages; move Chichewa-only attempt into primary analysis slots Chad School-language information can be split across FL9A and FL9B Construct a common lang_school field Zimbabwe Passage language requires multiple pieces of routing information Infer using school language, home language and story choice Nigeria, Eswatini, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, Zimbabwe Passage-language coding differs from single-language survey pattern Apply survey-specific passage-language rules These exceptions are the reason the reading file should be generated from the original UNICEF data rather than by blindly appending similarly named fields. 39.2 FS/background issues Survey/country Issue AFLEARN treatment Tunisia 2018 Some common FS themes/fields are absent Create harmonised columns as missing where appropriate DR Congo School-type coding uses a different network taxonomy Retain raw codes; document rather than force into standard categories Tunisia School-type “other” category differs from common coding Retain country coding and document Gambia School type unavailable in current harmonisation Missing Togo School type unavailable in current harmonisation Missing Sierra Leone Discipline attitude item is stored in a different source field Map the appropriate country-specific source Sierra Leone fl_child_result is absent in the current source layout Retain as missing Malawi Parent-education raw category meanings differ across mother/father fields Apply variable-specific education maps Tunisia 2018 Child-labour module absent Harmonised child-labour fields created as missing 39.3 Variables that retain country-specific meaning Even where no special code fix is required, some harmonised variables should not be interpreted as common cross-country categories. These include: region school_type raw education levels raw grade/year lang_home lang_school A common column name means: this is the analogous source concept in each survey not: every numeric category has exactly the same substantive meaning in every country. 39.4 Education-level maps AFLEARN does harmonise broad education levels into: 0 Early childhood / pre-primary 1 Primary 2 Lower secondary 3 Upper secondary 4 Vocational / technical 5 Higher / tertiary 8 Don't know 9 Other / missing special category But the country mapping required to reach those broad levels differs. Examples include: technical/vocational programmes embedded within secondary schooling; standalone vocational programmes; education systems without separately coded lower secondary; Tunisia adult-education/literacy categories; and Zimbabwe vocational and tertiary subtypes. Every raw-to-harmonised mapping is written to the level_map sheet. 39.5 Survey year matters Do not assume that one country-specific rule applies forever. If a country appears in multiple survey years: country + survey year should be treated as the unit for validating: questionnaire wording; variable names; coding; passage languages; education structure; and country-specific repairs. A new survey round should be reviewed even if the same country was supported previously. 39.6 How to add a new country safely Do not begin by writing a large block of special-case code. Use this sequence: 1. compare questionnaire with standard MICS6 questionnaire 2. inspect fs.sav and hl.sav variable names 3. run standard mappings 4. identify fields that fail or differ 5. add the smallest country-specific exception necessary 6. document the exception 7. validate distributions and published indicators A country-specific fix should be narrow enough that unexpected changes in a future source file trigger an error rather than silently producing a plausible-looking dataset.

Use the crosswalk to answer: What source variable supplied father education in each survey? Was it read from fs or linked from hl? Which raw codes map to primary, lower secondary, upper secondary, etc.? Does a country have a special category or missing-data rule? Is coverage materially different in a particular survey? This is especially important for variables that required construction rather than simple renaming. 40.3 What should be in a good crosswalk row? At minimum: theme harmonised_name harmonised_label survey source_file source_variable transformation notes The existing workbook already contains much of this information. As the revised guide develops, it would be useful to make source_file and transformation explicit wherever a variable is constructed from another file or recoded. 40.4 Reading crosswalk The reading script currently documents mappings primarily in code and in the existing technical guide. For long-term maintainability, AFLEARN should also provide a machine-readable reading crosswalk. A useful structure would be: country_iso3 year harmonised_variable passage source_variable transformation notes For example: MWI | 2019 | words_att | English | FL20A | rename | passage A MWI | 2019 | words_att | Chichewa | FLB20A | passage-specific processing | ... 41 Why current_grade is not the child’s grade current_grade looks like a grade variable, but it records the year within the child’s current education level. That distinction is easy to miss. Consider: current_level_h current_grade Meaning Primary 1 First year of primary Lower secondary 1 First year of lower secondary Upper secondary 1 First year of upper secondary All three children have: current_grade = 1 but they are at very different points in the school system. The same issue applies to: highest_grade previous_grade which should be interpreted with their corresponding education-level variables. 41.1 Why this happens The standard MICS schooling questions separately record: education level + grade/year within that level AFLEARN harmonises the level into: current_level_h but deliberately leaves current_grade as the year reported within that level. This preserves the source information rather than imposing a single grade system on countries with different education structures. 41.2 The “sawtooth” problem If you pool currently enrolled children and graph only current_grade, you will see many children at: 1, 2, 3 because primary, lower secondary and upper secondary cycles each restart. That distribution is not a simple Grade 1 → Grade 12 progression. Before using grade for trajectories, either: restrict the analysis to one education level; or construct a country-specific administrative grade. 41.3 Option 1: restrict to primary school For many foundational-learning analyses, the cleanest solution is: primary <- d %>% filter( enrolled == 1, current_level_h == 1 ) Within primary: current_grade = 1, 2, 3, ... has a much clearer interpretation. This is the approach used in the basic grade-trajectory example in Section 6. 41.4 Option 2: construct an administrative grade Suppose a country has: 6 years primary 3 years lower secondary 3 years upper secondary Then: d <- d %>% mutate( admin_grade = case_when( current_level_h == 1 ~ current_grade, current_level_h == 2 ~ 6 + current_grade, current_level_h == 3 ~ 9 + current_grade, TRUE ~ NA_real_ ) ) produces: Primary 1 admin_grade 1 ... Primary 6 admin_grade 6 Lower secondary 1 admin_grade 7 ... Upper secondary 3 admin_grade 12 41.5 Ghana example In the current MICS6 harmonised data, Ghana provides a clean example of a: 6 + 3 + 3 structure. The administrative-grade transformation is therefore: gha <- d %>% filter(country_iso3 == "GHA") %>% mutate( admin_grade = case_when( current_level_h == 1 ~ current_grade, current_level_h == 2 ~ 6 + current_grade, current_level_h == 3 ~ 9 + current_grade, TRUE ~ NA_real_ ) ) 41.6 Do not use the same offsets in every country Primary-cycle length differs across countries. The current source data include examples of: 5-year primary cycles 6-year primary cycles 7-year primary cycles 8-year primary cycles Some systems also code lower-secondary years differently or do not use a separate lower-secondary category in the same way. A correct administrative-grade variable therefore requires a country-specific education-system lookup. A useful future AFLEARN lookup would contain: country_iso3 survey_year current_level_h grade_within_level admin_grade notes source 41.7 Validate the constructed grade After constructing admin_grade, check: plausible ages by grade; weighted enrolment distribution; maximum grade against the education structure; transitions between education levels; and country documentation. For example: des %>% filter(enrolled == 1) %>% group_by(country_iso3, admin_grade) %>% summarise( mean_age = survey_mean( age, na.rm = TRUE ) ) A wildly non-monotonic age-by-grade profile is a sign that the grade construction needs review. 41.8 Grade is still not schooling exposure Even a correctly constructed administrative grade does not capture: repetition; late school entry; interrupted schooling; attendance; time through the current school year; or instructional time. For cross-country learning trajectories, Section 6 therefore also introduces gradeprogress, which adjusts grade approximately for the timing of the MICS interview within the school year. That variable answers a different problem and requires its own documented assumptions.

42 Validation and reproducibility 42.1 1. Structural checks 42.2 2. Range and coding checks 42.3 3. Routing checks 42.4 4. Cross-file merge checks 42.5 5. Compare with published MICS results 42.6 Reading-threshold validation 42.7 6. Validate multilingual reading separately 42.8 7. Survey-design checks 42.9 8. Version the scripts and outputs together 42.10 9. Keep raw data immutable 42.11 10. Minimum validation before adding a new survey

42 Validation and reproducibility A harmonisation script can run without errors and still produce the wrong data. AFLEARN therefore recommends validating at three levels: structural checks + distribution checks + external checks 42.1 1. Structural checks For every survey, verify: 42.1.1 Unique selected-child identifiers d %>% count(HH1, HH2, LN) %>% filter(n > 1) Expected: 0 rows 42.1.2 Expected survey size Compare the number of harmonised FS records with the original fs.sav. A harmonisation that unexpectedly drops children should fail loudly or report the exclusions explicitly. 42.1.3 Required fields Check that required variables exist: required <- c( "country_iso3", "year", "HH1", "HH2", "LN", "age", "fsweight" ) setdiff(required, names(d)) For the revised guide also require: PSU stratum 42.2 2. Range and coding checks Examples: range(d$age, na.rm = TRUE) table( d$current_level_h, useNA = "ifany" ) summary(d$fsweight) table( d$reading_status, useNA = "ifany" ) For reading: summary(reading$reading_accuracy) reading %>% filter(reading_accuracy > 1) Any accuracy above 1 requires investigation. For numeracy, after creating a total score: range(d$numeracy_total, na.rm = TRUE) should remain within: 0 to 21 42.3 3. Routing checks Variables should follow the questionnaire logic. Examples: children outside ages 7–14 → should not have a normal FLS reading outcome failed practice → should not have a valid main-passage score unless the country questionnaire legitimately permits it reading_status = attempted → should have a valid passage/score reading_status = foundational → should meet the underlying word/comprehension criteria Write these as automated tests where possible. For example: stopifnot( all( is.na(reading$reading_score[ reading$reading_status == 1 ]) ) ) Country exceptions should be documented rather than weakening the test globally. 42.4 4. Cross-file merge checks Whenever hl, hh, reading or IPUMS data are linked: confirm key uniqueness before the merge; report unmatched records; confirm the number of analysis rows after the merge; and compare key distributions before and after. Do not routinely discard _merge != 3 or unmatched rows without understanding them. 42.5 5. Compare with published MICS results For indicators that MICS itself publishes, reproduction is one of the strongest validation checks available. Examples include: foundational-reading classifications; foundational numeracy; school attendance; selected household/child characteristics. A discrepancy should trigger investigation of: denominator age restriction weight routing indicator definition rounding convention survey year rather than an immediate assumption that either source is wrong. 42.6 Reading-threshold validation AFLEARN’s rounded-down integer cutoff for the 90% reading-accuracy requirement was retained because alternative implementations were compared with published MICS classifications and the rounded-down convention reproduced those classifications. This should remain part of the regression test for the reading script. If a future edit changes the reading construction, rerun the country-level comparison against the MICS publications. 42.7 6. Validate multilingual reading separately For every multi-passage survey check: number attempting each passage passage-language distribution passage length multiple-attempt count reading-status distribution For Malawi, the validation should specifically confirm that Chichewa assessments are retained rather than disappearing from the analysis sample. 42.8 7. Survey-design checks Once PSU and stratum are retained in the FS harmonisation, check: d %>% summarise( missing_psu = sum(is.na(PSU)), missing_stratum = sum(is.na(stratum)) ) and: d %>% distinct( country_iso3, year, stratum, PSU ) %>% count( country_iso3, year, stratum, name = "n_psu" ) Unexpected single-PSU strata or missing design variables should be investigated against the country sampling documentation. 42.9 8. Version the scripts and outputs together A published harmonised dataset should identify the exact processing version used. For example: FS harmonisation v1.1 Reading harmonisation v1.2 Guide 2026-08 A useful release structure is: release/ ├── scripts/ ├── crosswalks/ ├── country-notes/ ├── validation/ └── README The validation directory can contain machine-readable summaries such as: survey_counts.csv reading_status_checks.csv published_indicator_comparison.csv merge_checks.csv 42.10 9. Keep raw data immutable The processing workflow should never edit the original UNICEF source files. A reproducible project keeps: raw source data ↓ processing scripts ↓ derived harmonised files so every result can be regenerated from the original inputs. 42.11 10. Minimum validation before adding a new survey Before a survey is added to the AFLEARN supported list: FS identifiers are unique. Key questionnaire variables have been checked against the survey questionnaire. Education-level mappings have been reviewed. Survey weights/design variables are present. Reading passage(s) and languages have been identified. Passage length has been validated. Reading routing has been checked. Reading classifications reproduce published results where available. Numeracy indicator reproduces published results if constructed. Crosswalk and country notes have been updated. No unexplained records fall into reading_status = 9. All output files regenerate cleanly from the scripts. This makes extending the guide slower than simply appending another country — but substantially safer.
